The Illuminator of the Essence of the Tantra Explaining the Five Jewels.
Salutation to Śiva. The Elucidation of the Essence of Tantra.
Having bowed to Śiva, who is worshipped by the illustrious Vīraṇa, I shall compose, in brief,
a commentary on the *Śrīpañcaratna* titled *Tantrasāraprakāśikā*.
Having bowed to the Lord, who is accompanied by Śakti, the cause of the six paths, the supreme and transcendent one;
I shall now describe the characteristics of the three accumulations of bound souls (paśu), which consist of bonds (pāśa), as well as those of the paths (adhvan).
Now, desiring to provide a concise commentary on this *Tantrasārapañcaratna* titled *Tantrasāraprakāśikā*,

[the author] first states the definition of the Lord (*pati*) with the words "Having bowed," etc. Having bowed to the Lord— the Supreme Śiva who is the essence of the category of the Lord— it is stated in the *Nārāyaṇopaniṣad*:
The Lord of the universe, the Self-sovereign, the eternal, the auspicious, and the infallible.
Likewise, in the illustrious *Kiraṇa*:
"In that same way, Śiva, the author of the entire world, remains as the source;
just as time, though it does not visibly transform, is seen to be the means for the production of results."
In this way, Śiva, though indeed formless, accomplishes his work by means of his will.
In the *Śrīmanmṛgendra*,
it is further stated: "When the property of being an effect is perceived,
one should know its agent to be distinct [from ordinary beings] through inference."
In the Pauṣkara [Sūtra], it is established for us both that the universe, which is the subject of dispute, is preceded by a creator who knows all things,
because it is an effect— just like a jar or other such effects.
It is characterized by the threefold activity consisting of abiding, enjoyment, and sovereignty.
An entity that is capable and does not deviate from its own nature is designated as the Lord (pati).
In the Parākhyatantra, objects are described as having form, possessing parts, and being characterized by various shapes and coverings.
Because gross substances remain as the residue [of analysis], they must have an intelligent cause.
Therefore, there exists some intelligent Lord who is eternally established.
In the *Viśvasārottara*, the Lord is established as the initiator of insentient things such as *māyā* and the rest;
he is the knower of all objects, the agent, the all-pervasive, and eternally manifest.

Thus, the meaning of the word *pati* (Lord) is well-established through all the various sections (*prakaraṇa*) of the scriptures (*sakalāgama*). Now, regarding the function of the Lord, the *Vṛddhajābālopaniṣad* states: "He is stainless, his nature is eternal, [he is] beyond speech and meditation, and he is to be known through all the scriptures."
In the *Śrī Mṛgendra*,
that body [of Śiva] consists of five mantras suitable for the fivefold acts— Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāma, and Ādya— which constitute the head and other parts.
The creation, sustenance, destruction, concealment, and liberation of the world.
For this [consciousness], that very [action] together with its factors and its fruit is to be known as the "task" (kṛtya).
Just as the sun [attains] the lotus in the Pauṣkara [world] through constant acts such as awakening and drying it up,
so too does Śiva attain [the state] here through the activities known as "awakening."
From the agitation of the bindu of Śambhu, Śakti herself proceeds.
That [power] as well, consisting of knowledge and action, is the truth(s);
He is the Lord, the sovereign form of Śiva himself, who is in reality non-dual.
Now he states the nature of the inherent power (*samaveta-śakti*): "Having bowed to that which possesses inherent power.
In the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad*: "Its supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold; it is innate, consisting of knowledge, strength, and action. In the *Mṛgendra*:
The instrument is neither something other than power, nor is power something other than the accumulation of consciousness;
because of the restriction of the object, it is so in the case of a single cognition and likewise in action.
The power within the Three Jewels, consisting of an unobstructed mass of vast rays of light,
is considered to be consciousness itself— the undecaying majesty of the Supreme Lord.
In the Pauṣkara [treatise], it is said: "The pervasive, eternal, immovable, and all-facing Lord resides therein;
within Him, there is the pure consciousness alone, possessing attributes such as pervasiveness."
"And that power is non-different from Him; Śiva abides through inherence," and so forth.

Now he describes the nature of pure *māyā*: "Having bowed to the supreme (*paramām*), most excellent (*utkṛṣṭām*), or transcendent (*parām*) Kuṇḍalinī, who is the cause of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhva-hetum*), the source (*nidānabhūtām*) of the six paths beginning with the phonemes (*varṇa*)," as stated in the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad*: "One should know that *māyā* is indeed primordial nature (*prakṛti*)."
In the Pauṣkara [Tantra], Vāgīśvarī is called Parāvidyā, Kuṭilā, Kuṇḍalī, Parā,
Śuddhamāyā, and the Supreme Bindu; she is described as Śabdabrahman.
That which is born from the Three Jewels, wherein it exists pure, and wherein it dissolves—that is the *bindu* called Supreme Sound (*paranāda*). It is not merely sound and drop (*nādabindu*);
it is the bulb (*kanda*), supreme bliss, Śiva, the eternally arisen Lord.
Neither setting nor rising, neither weary nor subject to transformation,
the Sun whose essence is the Word-Brahman moves within all beings.
In the Pauṣkara,
it is stated that the channel-kuṇḍalinī of Śambhu’s power is pure yet insentient by nature;
she does not abide through identity [with the Lord], but rather exists within His embrace.
Because Śiva is the agent, this Kuṇḍalinī exists through identity with him.
Because it is the material cause, just as clay is in the case of a potter;
its mode of existence consists of reality itself, and it is established in four ways.
The Śiva-tattva is called Sadeśa, as well as Īśa and that which is named Vidyā.
"These principles are pure for the great-souled Rudrāṇus," and so forth.

Now, the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* describes the state of the supreme (*parā*) [condition]: "One should meditate upon speech as a cow; she has four udders, and her calves are breath, sight, hearing, and mind."

In the *Viśvasārottara*, it is said that she has four modes of speech (*vāgvṛtti*) whose primary form is *vaikharī*: *vaikharī*, *madhyamā*, another called *paśyantī*, and the subtle one known as *sūkṣmā*. According to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), *parā* is said to reside in the *mūlādhāra*, *paśyantī* is situated in the heart, and *madhyamā* is in the region of the throat.

"Vaikharī [speech] resides in the palate and the cavity of the lips; [the subtle speech] resides in the head at the Pauṣkara [lotus], and the intermediate sound resides in the *śiras* [the top of the head]. These words, situated in the impure path, exist as increasingly grosser than the gross. And so forth.

Now he describes the arising of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*). In the *Mahopaniṣad*: "May I attain the end of the paths, of the Lord of Paths, the most excellent path. In the *Svāyaṃbhuvatantra*: "The effects (*kāryāṇi*) are proclaimed as the names of those six paths."
The path of phonemes, the path of words, the path of mantras, and the path of worlds.
The path of reality (tattvādhvan) and the path of limited agency (kalādhvan)—these are considered the six paths.
Among those, three are known as having the form of sound (śabda), and three are remembered as having the form of meaning (artha).
Here, the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) is fully described as the collection of fifty phonemes.
The eighty-one *padas* alone are called the *padādhvan* (the path of words);
the *mantrādhvan* (the path of mantras) is said to consist of the five *brahmas*, the *aṅgas*, and the six [mantras].
Two hundred and twenty-four worlds constitute the world-meaning.
Endowed with thirty-six principles, it is proclaimed as the path of reality (tattvādhvan).
Śāntyatītā, Śānti, along with Vidyā and Pratiṣṭhā,
and Nivṛtti— thus, through this division, the path of Kalās is declared to be fivefold.

Likewise, in the *Tātparya-saṃgraha*, it is stated that [the scripture] speaks of the path, the Lord of the Path, the gradations within the path, and the successful journey to the end of the supreme path. Maheśvara, the author of the *Gṛhyakāra*, says:
"Of the paths... and so forth, beginning with the statement that the father, having initiated the boy (*kumāra*), addressed him with these words.
Now, he describes the nature of Māyā below: in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad it says, "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti.
Likewise, in the Svāyaṃbhuva [Tantra]: "The principle of Māyā is the seed of the universe, indestructible, and of the nature of Śiva."
[He perceives] the Lord, who is all-pervading, subtle, beginningless, and imperishable.
In the *Mṛgendra*, [the categories] beginning with the knot (*granthi*) are: *kalā*, time (*kāla*), knowledge (*vidyā*), passion (*rāga*), the human (*nṛ*),
the mother (*mātṛ*), the qualities (*guṇa*), attainment (*adhigama*), pride (*garva*), mind (*citta*), the senses (*akṣa*), and the bound soul (*paśu*), in their respective order.
Likewise, in the Pauṣkara [Tantra]:
"Time, Necessity, and Kalā are directly born from Māyā. And in the Raurava [Tantra]:
From the principle of *kalā* arise *rāga* and *vidyā*; these two are its [functions].
In the Pauṣkara,
the Puruṣa is proclaimed as being joined with the five coverings (kañcukas), intent upon enjoying Prakṛti, and associated with ignorance (avidyā) and the other [afflictions].
Now, that which has come down through the lineage is being examined. And because it arises from Māyā, it has attained grossness from Kalā. In the *Kiraṇa*, [it is said]:
"From the supreme sovereign of the kings of the universe (*viśvarājādhirāja*), the King of Mantras..."
And indeed, by the power of Śiva’s Śakti, Ananta is awakened.
In the Pauṣkara [Tantra]:
Now, from the principle of Prakṛti, the principle of the Guṇas was born;
[he who is] the agitator is Śrīkaṇṭha of infinite prowess.
O best of sages, from the principle of the qualities (guṇatattva) arose the supreme intellect (parābuddhi);
beyond this, the principle of ego (ahaṃkāratattva) is described.
And that [ego] is taught to be threefold; among them, the first is the taijasa (fiery), the second would be the vaikārika (modifying), and the other is the bhūtādika (elemental).
From the taijasa ego as well, the mind, the intellect, and the sense organs [arise].
The five organs of action arise from the modified ego (vaikṛta-ahaṃkāra).
From the ego (ahaṃkāra), however, arises the aggregate of the subtle elements (tanmātras) starting with the gross elements;
from the fivefold group of subtle elements, the great elements (mahābhūtāni) are produced in succession.

"In Mataṅga, those who dwell within Māyā are called 'bound souls' (paśu), characterized by bondage," and so forth. Now, he states the definition of the bound soul: "I shall declare the definition of the three collections of bound souls."

In the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad: The eternal Self is bound by its state of being an enjoyer; having known God, one is released from all fetters. In the Kiraṇa [Tantra]: The Paśu is eternal, indeed formless and knowing, inactive, devoid of qualities, yet the Lord; pervasive, situated within the belly of Māyā, he is the one who contemplates the means of experience.
In the Pauṣkara,
it is said that a bound soul (paśu), because of its connection with the state of being a bound soul, is called a "bound soul" (paśu); for,
although devoid of the [limited] power (kalā), he possesses his own specific activities and is not the Lord.
In the Siddhāntaśekhara it is said: "The individual soul (puruṣa) is eternal, ignorant, dependent on another, the agent, the enjoyer, and a bound creature (paśu)."

Now he states the classification of the bound souls (paśu): "In the causal state, the bound souls are to be known as threefold—the Sakala, the Pralayākala, and the Vijñānākala; their characteristics are now described."
The distinction among those beginning with the *sakala* arises from the specific nature of their bondage by fetters (*pāśa*).
One who is conjoined with the fetters of *māyā*, *karman*, and *mala* is known as the *sakala*.
Bound by the two nooses of impurity (mala) and karma is the *pralayākala*; that which is joined with the single noose of impurity is called the *vijñānākala*.
Among those known as the Vijñānākala, who are bound by a single impurity (mala) of Pauṣkara,
some become pure within the range of perception only after awaiting the ripening of that impurity.

In the domains of the three powers (*yodaja*), you [the yogin] conquer some who are intense through their vision and action in the principle called *bhoga*, and others in the principle called *īśvara*.
I invoke others who are all-knowing and powerful within the reality called Vidya;
they are subject to the ripening of their impurities and are the eight presiding authorities in the Kṣutīṣṭha.
Endowed with bodies of the bindu, possessed of omniscience,
and gifted with the qualities of Sadāśiva, they are great universal emperors,
characterized by supreme beauty and charm, as well as by a tranquil mind.
By virtue of their respective offices, the powers of Śambhu’s limited agency perform the acts of maintaining,
protecting, bestowing, and showing grace toward worldly existence.
In the principle of Īśvara is Vāsanta; Māyā belongs to those who hold office within the womb [of the universe]. Among them, Ananta is the first, followed by Sūkṣma and Śivottama.
Then, in sequence, come Ekanetra, Ekarudra, and Trimūrti;
and below them, Śrīkaṇṭha and Śikhaṇḍī, each possessing progressively diminished power.
For whoever is superior in qualities over another is considered to be above him.
Likewise, Śiva alone creates the other Lords of Mantras who dwell in the principle of Vidyā; they are seven crores in number.
They are the lords of the mantras that constitute the performance of initiation.
These Lords of Mantras are said to be those who act for the benefit of the worlds;
yet, although they are omniscient, these Lords of Mantras possess progressively lesser powers as they descend lower and lower.

The three [powers], being dependent on the body, exercise their authority throughout the entire path; at the end of that duration, they enter into Śiva along with the Lord. (**) The three powers: *icchā* (will), *jñāna* (knowledge), and *kriyā* (action).

Without a formal legal proceeding (*adhikaraṇa*), one does not [attain the goal]; having set aside the subordinate section (*vikṛti*) and completed the primary section (*adhikāra*), he proceeds to his own path once it has been withdrawn. By virtue of the ripening of impurities (*mala-pāka*), he becomes fit and endowed with the grace of Śiva. (**) Note: The symbol (*) likely refers to a specific ritual or technical term within the source text. The symbol (**) indicates a lacuna or a missing portion in the original manuscript. The translation reflects the context of Śaiva Siddhānta ritual and soteriology.
Thus, seventy million [souls] have been liberated above; however,
those who possess unripened impurities among those called *vijñānākala* remain as mere impurity until the end of the ripening of that impurity.
At times, through their arts and their actions,
those very same eminent sages become directly manifest as those who possess pure discriminative knowledge (*vijñāna-kevala*).
Those possessed of authority and yet endowed with impurity are always considered [as such] by Śiva.
Now, among those previously designated as *pralayākala*,
those whose impure karma has fully ripened go [to their respective states].
Likewise, O Lord of Mantras, when others have been bound by impurity and karma within the names of the Pralayākalas, according to the ripening of their impurities;
And those who belong to the stage of the womb of Māyā, having their impurities and karma removed by Śiva-initiation performed by the supreme Lords of Mantra, [attain liberation].
Together with Kalā and the others who preside over the womb of Māyā, they are joined with bodies born of that [Māyā] and are rendered subject to its control.
The Lord of lords makes them the lords of the worlds; they are the Pañcāṣṭakas and so forth.
In the Kāmika [Tantra], there are the Pakvatripās, as well as the Sakalas and the Pakvatriśakas.
The Krodhas and others are the Maṇḍalins, and likewise the others are the Śatarudras.
Śrīkaṇṭha and Vīrabhadra are remembered as having their three bonds matured;
others, whose bonds are undiminished, are remembered as bound transmigrators in Raurava.
These are declared to be the hundred Rudras, situated all around the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) in succession.
The Rudras previously mentioned stand for the purpose of guarding the ten directions;
they are traditionally taught as being ten by ten, respectively, in each individual direction.
Presided over by Śrīkaṇṭha, the hundred Rudras of great majesty bestowed upon the progenitors of beings,
beginning with Brahmā, a sovereign power equal to their own that was impossible for others to pierce.
The high-souled ones of immeasurable power bestow [these] upon the gods;
those people are also said to be known by the names of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra. And these, such as Vīrabhadra and others, are devoid of the quality of *māyā*.
He is known as Vīrabhadra, likewise the lord of the hundred Rudras;
those eight Maṇḍalin-s are the Kalās residing upon his head.
Likewise, the eight [deities] beginning with Krodha are situated above the Guṇatattva;
Śrīkaṇṭha resides within the Guṇatattva, and below him is the Lord of the World (Bhuvanādhipa).
He is the cause of their origination, dissolution, maintenance, and grace.
In the Pauṣkara, the nature of the bound soul (paśu) has been stated; now the nature of the fetter (pāśa) is being described.
Now he states the definition of the nooses: "I shall explain the definition of the three [categories] whose nature is that of the nooses."

In the *Kiraṇa*, it is said that this state of being a bound soul (*paśutva*) resides within the self; even the bound soul (*paśu*) exists within the midst of the paths (*adhvan*). Therefore, impurity (*mala*) has been described as having a characteristic distinct from that [state of bondage].
Impurity, ignorance, the state of being a bound soul (paśutva), the darkness that causes obscuration,
nescience (avidyā), and the covering— these are declared to be its synonyms.
In the *Mṛgendra*, that one [principle] is the beginningless, dense, and great source of all beings;
it resides within each individual soul, extending to its own creative power (*kalā*), like a collection of the powers of wind.
"In the *Svāyaṃbhuvatantra*, beginningless impurity (*anādimala*) is proclaimed as the state of bondage (*paśutva*) for souls;
it should be understood as being like the husk and the pod of the sprout of the seed of *māyā*. Thus it is said, and so forth.
Now, the *Pauṣkara* describes the fetter consisting of *māyā*:"
Because the entire universe emerges from this, it is called *māyā*;
yet, in its own essential nature, *māyā* does not exist as a causal agent for persons.
Because they are assisted by atoms through their effects, this [agency] does not belong to the selves.
In the doctrine of the Supreme (Parākhyā), the agent and so forth are accepted as the means for accomplishing the purpose of the atom.
It is also determined by the distinction of individual experience, which is restricted to each person.
Thus, in the system of Svayambhū, the individual soul (aṇu), residing in the world and obscured by its own defects,
becomes absorbed in those illusory enjoyments, being colored by attachment to them.
From Śiva, the *kalā* comes into connection with that pure [soul] as its cause; by means of *kalā*,
consciousness is set in motion, and its sphere of experience is revealed by *vidyā*.
Furthermore, colored by passion— which is essentially the primary quality (sattva)—
the bound soul (paśu) is fettered through its connection with the array of instruments, beginning with the intellect (buddhi).
Then, through the connection with destiny (niyati), one is constrained within what has been acquired by oneself;
deluded regarding one's portion, one is governed by time according to the calculation of time.
Thus, bound by the *kalās* of reality, possessing limited knowledge and joined with a body, embraced by the enjoyment of *māyā*, identified with that, and shrouded by his innate nature; |||
Śiva (*), due to his own karma, experiences the enjoyment of suffering and so forth.
Now he speaks of the bond of karma; in the *Viśvasārottara*:
"Karma consists of dharma and adharma, and it is threefold in its essential nature:
that which bestows birth, lifespan, and experience, by means of which one ripens nowhere in a mixed state."
Just as its impurity is beginningless, so too its karma is beginningless.
If it were not beginningless, by what cause would this diversity be established?
In the *Mṛgendra*, it is stated that the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*)— being produced by the operation of karma— is subtle by nature;
it is the generator and sustainer of fortune, and consists of the three means beginning with the internal (*adhyātma*).
Because it originates from that which is both true and false, [the world] consists of the nature of dharma and adharma;
it reaches its fruition during [the Lord's] sleep, at which time its creator is disjoined from it.
Now he states the definition of the three times (*adhva*): "I shall explain the definition of the three times.
In the *Mataṅga*: "Of the principles (*tattva*) beginning with water and ending with the qualities (*guṇa*), each subsequent one..."
The increase should be known as tenfold, reaching up to a hundred crores because of its reality.
The remaining qualities mentioned in the teaching are said to be one hundred and more.
The principles (tattvas) end with Māyā; from them, the principle [of Śuddhavidyā] is a thousandfold.
Up to the principle of Sadāśiva, that which is beyond it is designated as the "Lakṣa" (the Hundred Thousand).
The group of four culminates in Śānti; beyond this, the object of knowledge is Paraśiva.

Likewise, in the *Siddhāntasārāvalī*: "The earth-tattva is one hundred crore yojanas; starting from the waters up to the end of the Gonas, the calculation is by tens; likewise, from Prakṛti down to the end of Māyā, it is one hundred [crores]."

And he, whose power is immeasurable, pervades from the thousand-fold [universe] up to Sadāśiva, extending for a hundred thousand [yojanas] until the very end; beyond that, he is the presiding lord of the Bindu.

In the Kāmika [Tantra], the pure path (śuddhādhvan) is said to originate from the Bindu; for those whose nature is defiled by impurity (mala), it extends up to Māyā. Beyond that, the mixed path (miśrādhvan) belongs to those characterized by both impurity and karma.

The pure path (śuddhādhvan) is proclaimed as belonging to those who possess all [powers] (sakala). In the *Kiraṇa*, it is stated that Śiva is the agent on the pure path, while the Lord is the agent on the path that is not white [i.e., the impure].
"In Pauṣkara, Śrīkaṇṭha resides within the principle of Guṇatattva; below that is the Lord of the World," and so forth.
Furthermore, by the word "atha" (now), he speaks regarding the characteristic of the descent of the power of withdrawal (*saṃhāra-śakti-pāta*).
In the *Mṛgendra*, it is stated that for both types of practitioners on the two paths,
there is an emanation in direct order and a dissolution in reverse order, extending up to the two principles of Śakti.
In the Pauṣkara [Purāṇa],
it is stated that the elements reside in the subtle elements (tanmātras), the subtle elements in the ego (ahaṃkāra),
the senses and the mind in the intellect (buddhi), and the intellect in the qualities (guṇas).

The three qualities (guṇas) dissolve into primordial nature (prakṛti), and that [nature], along with the pentad of principles beginning with passion (rāga), dissolves into Māyā; yet she (Māyā) is established as eternal.
Above Māyā, the pure path desires dissolution into the Bindu;
the Bindu consists of Kalā and the other [categories], is of the nature of Śakti, and has its form presided over by Śiva.
It remains eternally before this Śiva as the essence of his own object;
then the universe proceeds again, beginning from the *bindu*.
Thus, in the *Tattvaprakāśa*: "In the dissolution of objects, this triad—Māyā, Puruṣa, and Śiva—remains;
then, however, that [triad] proceeds again in the prior creation."
Even while the Lord of Beasts is asleep, he remains awakening those capable of being awakened, restraining those who must be restrained, and causing the agent to perform his duty.
Making the power of illusion (māyā-śakti) render all things fit for manifestation, he perceives every category of object exactly as it is.
In the *Kāmika*, it is said that at the time of creation and dissolution, the power of obstruction (*rodhaśakti*), whose essence is Śiva,
falls downward for the sake of liberating bound souls (*paśu*) whose fetters have been ripened.
Now he states the definition of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), as given in the *Mṛgendra*:
"For those embodied beings upon whom the Power descends so that they do not return [to transmigratory existence],
the sign of that is an eagerness for liberation and an aversion to remaining in worldly existence."
Devotion toward the devotees of Śiva, and faith in the ritual prescribed by his teaching.
In the Pauṣkara [Tantra],
it is said that when the karma that destroys [the cycle] ripens as the fruition of even impurity (mala),
the power of Unmīlinī, which effects grace, descends as a cooperative cause.
As soon as that [impurity] has fallen away, the restraining power (niyāmikā-śakti) of the impurity ceases; once that has ceased, [liberation occurs] for those great-souled ones.
Detachment from the ocean of suffering that is saṃsāra arises quickly,
and a longing to behold the lotus feet of Śambhu also arises.
"How shall I behold the Lord of Gods? How shall I be released from this bondage?
Who indeed will show me Śambhu?"—such was the thought that arose within him.
If the Lord thus bestows grace upon one who is terrified of saṃsāra, [then he is truly the Lord].
Such details have not been written here for fear of prolixity.
Having undergone initiation and purified his body by performing the ritual placements (*nyāsa*) with the true principles (*tattva*), he should draw a lotus;
then, displaying the *nalinī* mudrā, he should worship the Lord, whose *liṅga* is situated upon the glorious lotus-throne.

Now the Kriyāpāda begins—[concerning] initiation (*dīkṣā*). In the *Yajurvedopaniṣad*: "The teacher is the prior form; the student is the subsequent form; knowledge is the connection. [As stated] in the *Siddhāntaśiromaṇi*.
Thus requested by the pure disciple, the supreme guru,
having observed the descent of power (śaktipāta), should unite him with initiation (dīkṣā).
In the Svāyambhuva [Manvantara], his self was bound by these principles (tattvas), and he was endowed with all dharmas.
No one else is able to release it; once released, it is of the nature of Śiva through initiation.
In Mataṅga, distinguished knowledge is bestowed and the accumulation of bonds is destroyed;
that by which initiation occurs, arising from the impurity of the activity of Māyā, is considered [the specific type of initiation].
In the Siddhāntaśekhara, it is stated:
"This initiation is divided into two kinds: that which has a support and that which is devoid of a support. That which is performed by Śaṅkara himself is carried out even without a preceptor."
Through the descent of the intense power (tīvra-śakti-nipāta), initiation is attained for those known as Vijñānākala and Pralayākala, excluding the common [initiation].
Relying upon the form of the Guru, by means of causing the descent of the subtle power (manda-śakti), the Lord effects this [descent] for everyone up to the end of the common level; this they know.

The common [practice] is said to be threefold: with seed-syllables, with seed-syllables and symbols, and [without]. These are clearly manifested in the sections on ritual action, devotion, and knowledge, respectively.
The world with its seeds is twofold: that characterized by worldly phenomena and that characterized by the auspicious.
All accumulated unrighteousness, which follows from karma, is purified therein.
Where that initiation consists of worldly phenomena, it remains merely a residue of dharmas.
The Śivadharmiṇī is of two kinds: the material (bhautikī) and the lifelong (naiṣṭhikī).
That which is joined with the formal release from the vow is called "temporary" (bhautikī);
that vow which lasts until the fall of the body is considered "lifelong" (nauṣṭhikī).
Now, the twofold division of seedless initiation (nibīja-dīkṣā) is declared:
the first bestows immediate liberation (sadyo-nirvāṇadā), while the other bestows liberation after some time (ciraṃ-nirvāṇadā).
The web of karma— consisting of that which has begun to bear fruit (*prārabdha*), that which has been accumulated (*sañcita*), and that which is yet to come (*āgāmi*)—
is purified for those who feel revulsion toward the body and its like through the most intense maturation [of wisdom].
That [knowledge] bestows immediate liberation upon those who are utterly dispassionate;
yet, for those with *prārabdha* karma, it grants liberation immediately after the exhaustion of that experience.
Fools and others go [to their destruction]; may this [initiation] grant them long-lasting nirvāṇa.
There is the initiation of touch for the eyes, as well as the verbal and the mental.
And the initiation into yoga through scripture; thus, it is proclaimed to be sixfold.
Having opened his eyes and meditated upon that reality, he gazes at the disciple;
for the sake of liberating him from the bonds of the fetters, this is the initiation by the eye (cākṣuṣī-dīkṣā).
Having placed Śiva, conjoined with the Brahma-aṅgas, in his right hand, he should touch the disciple’s head; this shall be the initiation by touch (sparśadīkṣā).
Having concentrated the mind upon that reality, illuminated by the splendor of the Lord, one should utter the Saṃhitā mantras; this is proclaimed as the initiation of speech (vāgdīkṣā).
Relying upon a mental procedure, it is designated as "mental."
The initiation into the scripture (*śāstradīkṣā*) is proclaimed to occur through the transmission of the scripture;
the initiation born of yoga (*yogajā*) arises from the transmission of the *Tattvadyota*.
Furthermore, that [initiation] becomes sevenfold through the distinctions of the *ājñā*-initiation and so forth:
the *ājñā*, the *upamā*, the *svastikā*, and the supreme *kalaśasnapanā*.
She who is dependent on the manifestation of power yet remains self-dependent—these seven are proclaimed;

The comparison is considered to be similar to the traditional practice of the predecessors.
Having placed the disciple upon the *svastika* by means of the Guru’s rite of protection (*rakṣaṇakarma*),

The initiation consisting of the cloth of prosperity (bhūtipaṭṭa), which is proclaimed as being performed with ashes,
is [bestowed] by the gurus upon the forehead of the disciple according to the path of traditional practice (samayācāra).
The preceptor, having taken up the insignia and worshipped it according to the prescribed rite,
is declared to be fully authorized for the formal initiation of the disciple.
Then, having bowed down and accepted the *liṅga* with devotion, the disciple should wear it upon his head and other parts of his body, declaring, "It is now under the control of my Guru."
Furthermore, that [tradition], consisting of various divisions and sub-divisions, is of two kinds:
of these, the first is endowed with knowledge (jñānavatī), and the second is endowed with ritual action (kriyāvatī).
The initial action, consisting of specialized knowledge and so forth, is performed by the Guru alone with a mind endowed with such qualities;
it is carried out for the sake of the purification of the specific impurities.

Another [form] is called "seedless" (nirbījā), which is associated with ritual action and consists of the sacrificial pit, the mandala, and so forth, and is joined with various divisions and subdivisions.
Initiation that imparts knowledge is proclaimed to be composed of consciousness.
Thus, the many kinds of common [initiations] have been briefly described.
In the *Mṛgendra*, it is said that for a living being whose impurity has been touched by the fire of initiation, his own power becomes manifest through yoga.
Once the region of the heart has been kissed by the Power of the All-pervading Lord, it does not turn away from Him toward any other man.

One should always place the two principles, Śiva and Īśvara, within the mouths.
One should place Vidyā and Mohinī, as well as Kāla and Kalā,
Avidyā and Niyati, and Rāga within the heart; likewise, one should place Puruṣa, Prakṛti, Buddhi, and Ahaṅkāra.
The mind, the ear, the skin, the eye, the tongue, and likewise the breath; the organ of speech, the hands, the feet, the anus, and the generative organ as well.
One should place sound, touch, form, taste, and likewise smell, as well as space, wind, fire, and water, into the secret [center].
One should also place the single principle of earth (pṛthivī-tattva) upon the pair of feet;
thus is described the deposition of the thirty-six principles as proclaimed in the Śaiva Āgamas.
"The principles (tattvas) beginning with earth are the abodes of experience for embodied beings;

together with the worlds, they are to be purified by means of the sequential method, in whatever manner [is appropriate]," and so forth. Now, he describes the lotus mandala: "having drawn the lotus," etc.

From the earth element up to water is the *kanda*; the earth is known as the lake.

who dwells in conduct (*ācāra*), in the divine *liṅga*, and who alone occupies the station of his own incomparable devotees.
When the nose is the mouth and the mind is the hand, and the dense [substance] is joined with the power of action as the cause of bliss,

one who has offered even the smelled substance— which is the object of the ritual act— as prescribed by the injunction, being generally full of true devotion, should here himself partake of this grace of fragrance.

Upon this [liṅga] established on his own body— the supreme Guru-liṅga, well-known as being in the mouth and tongue, impelled by the incomparable innate power of knowledge, and whose nature is Maheśvara— the wise man,
with a hand consisting of firm devotion, spiritual power, and a most great intellect directed toward it, [attains liberation].
Having offered the flavorful substance, one should personally partake of the prasāda known as the stainless essence.

I, endowed with devotion and characterized by attentive mindfulness, [bow] with humility before that very Linga called Śiva— the eternally gracious one, who has attained the supreme state, whose divine limbs are manifest, who employs the power of his own will, and who is present in the world and in the face through the hand he has fashioned.
Having surrendered the portion to be seen, one should enjoy the grace of the form established through that surrender.

With his mind fixed through the vital breath (*prāṇa*) upon the *liṅga* situated in the body, and having offered the object of touch (*spraṣṭavya*) to this very *liṅga* called "movement" (*cara*)— which resides in the skin, in the world, and in [the senses] such as the mouth when impelled by power— he, endowed with the power of devotion born of his own direct experience, [attains the goal].
The knower of reality should constantly cultivate contact with clarity and unsurpassed bliss.

Having offered everything here into the ear and mouth— which are joined with the Supreme Power (Parāśakti)— within the Liṅga, which is manifest grace and established as the limb known as the Pure Refuge (Vimalaśaraṇa),
this very [devotee], through the hand of supreme knowledge, possesses devotion whose form is bliss and which is intensely radiant.
Abiding in the supreme refuge, one should personally and incessantly enjoy that grace known as sound.

In the great *liṅga* which is the limb of oneness, endowed with the Great Power of Consciousness within the heart and the mouth, one should offer devotion through constant feeling and the hand; for the Self, which is itself Being-Consciousness, is that which must be known.
Having offered what is to be known, the pure-minded one must necessarily offer that which is to be offered.
"Therefore, one should cultivate that pure, dense, and highly refined clarity which has been attained. And so forth.
Now, he describes the inner worship (*antar-pūjā*) in the *Siddhāntaśiromaṇi*:
"In the abode of the heart, which is the lamp of consciousness, [situated] at the nine gates of the sense organs of cognition..."
Seated upon a lotus throne, he is the individual soul (cilliṅga), the very embodiment of Śiva.
Having meditated at all times, one should worship the Bhāva with ritual substances;
the water of the consecration is forbearance, and discernment is said to be the garment.
Truth is said to be the ornament; detachment is the flower garland;
the attainment of meditative absorption is the fragrance; and the absence of egoism is the unbroken rice grains.
Faith is the incense; great wisdom is the lamp that illuminates the world;
and the offering of that which is the root of delusion—the manifold conceptual proliferation—is the food offering.
Silence is the bell, movement is the offering of sensory objects;
the absence of delusion regarding those objects is conceived as circumambulation.
The power inherent in the intellect is considered to be the act of salutation;
thus, by means of such metaphorical expressions established as real entities, which are free from fault.
Without turning one's face away, one should worship the Liṅga within.
In the Vātūlottara, it is said:
"Knowledge is not devoid of action, nor is action devoid of knowledge;
the blind man who does not see is burned, and the lame man who sees is also burned."
"Therefore, practice consisting of wisdom and action should be performed by the wise," and so forth;
it is not written here for fear of prolixity.
Thus, being dependent on the dissolution of the mind,
that wise man, having heard from the words of his guru regarding Haṭhayoga and Rājayoga, should practice the Śaiva restraint (yama) which bestows liberation.

In the Siddhāntaśekhara:

when "so'haṃ so'ham" is attained, that is called Mantrayoga.

Regarding the phrase "dependent on the wind" (*adhīnavāta*): in the *Yogasaṃgraha*, it is stated:
"By means of the six actions, the three bonds, the eight limbs, and the eight suppressions..."
Hatha Yoga, which brings the vital breaths under control, is said to consist of ten mudrās. That [state] is called Tāra;
it is the King born of Yoga, the blazing, supreme, and imperishable Brahman.

He who is a practitioner of Haṭhayoga, who has mastered his breath through the eightfold path, the performance of mudrās, and various bodily postures, is a true master of the body.
He who, among three hundred thousand [beings], shall attain the direct realization of Brahman,
or who knows Rajayoga, being free from mental fluctuations— I know him.

The practitioner of Haṭhayoga and Rājayoga, having restrained the mind within the cavity of the heart (*śrāpaka*) by means of the moon and the sun through the path of the triangle, [attains] the eighteen [internal states] by means of those [practices] directed toward the external and internal.

If everyone says that victory comes by means of a sword, what then?"

"But when one is joined to that which is inexpressible, supportless, ungraspable, devoid of measure, and free from all essential natures, he is liberated; such is the certainty of the scripture."

All the senses, together with their powers (*bhūti*), are produced [from Him]; He is not a cause [in the sense of being a material cause], but rather He is the object of meditation, endowed with all sovereignty, the Lord of All, Śambhu, who dwells in the midst of space.
Thus is the first [chapter] called the *Atharva-cūḍā*, the *Atharva-śikhā*, its Heart, and that very darkness (*tamaḥ*).
That which is its abode is the heart; that pair is light beyond darkness. When seen in water, one becomes dual.
The moist burns. This is in the mirror. The eye, indeed, is Brahman.
That person who is in the right eye—that is the Self in the eye. This very Self...
One worships Vaiśvānara as the Person (Puruṣa), the Supreme Self (Paramātman). The Person is of the measure of a thumb; for the divine Person is formless.
The Person is the light within the heart. He alone is the Self described as "not this, not this" (neti neti), ungraspable. Indeed, the Self is one.
He is to be meditated upon: the Supreme Self, the witness of all actions, the conscious self, the Person (*puruṣa*).

"The Person, dark and tawny"—the Person is the Supreme Self. For this Self is in the heart; for all this is Brahman, and this Self is Brahman. That [Brahman] is to be worshipped within that [Self]. Indeed, all this is Brahman.

The Puruṣa alone is all this. That Puruṣa who is established on the tip of the thumb—he is this fire residing within the water. As the Great Lord of all worlds, he protects the entire world from the water. He is indeed this Puruṣa in the waters;
because he delivers one from the great fear of saṃsāra, he is called Tāra. "Homage to Tāra! thus [it is said].

I praise—that is, I laud—this Supreme Śiva, who is the Tāraka Brahman, whom all the Upaniṣads declare to be Śiva; who is the final conclusion of all philosophical systems; and who, as one's own chosen deity, is the side of truth for all people. "I" is the understood subject. This [is] the Gāyatrī of the thirty-two Upaniṣads of the four Vedas.
The secret meaning is to be understood from the instruction of the Teacher, the Elephant.
"That knowledge is to be known from a true guru, and not otherwise even by means of millions of scriptures," and so forth. It has not been written out here for fear of prolixity.
Mounted upon a swan, dwelling in a lotus, Lord of Speech, the Creator of the universe, the Protector of all, beloved of the one whose abode is the lotus, reclining upon Śeṣa, Śiva,
whose mouth is the lotus of his own heart, and the husband of the daughter of Himavat— [I bow] to him.
And Śambhu alone is the one who knows all things equally; I know everything that has a name.

Now, the previously mentioned Supreme Śiva, who is indeed one, is said to be divided threefold through the distinctions of Ātmabhū, Svabhū, and Bhava: "Haṃsa," etc. That one Śambhu is mounted upon the *haṃsa* (the vital breath), resting in the lotus, having his abode in the heart-lotus, the Lord of Speech, beloved of the supreme power (*parā-śakti*), [and] the universe...
"He creates" means the Creator of the Universe (*viśvasṛṭ*). This has been stated in the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad*:

"Having known Him who is subtler than the subtlest, in the midst of the waters, the creator of the universe, possessing manifold forms, the one who encompasses the universe—having known Śiva, one attains ultimate peace."

Elsewhere, the meaning is even more explicit: He who is Śambhu; the beloved of the lotus-dwelling [Brahmā]; the splendor of the Supreme Power (Parā-Śakti) residing in the heart-lotus; resting upon the couch of Śeṣa; situated above the Kuṇḍalinī power; the protector and guardian of all. As it has been said:
In the *Niśvāsakārikā*, it is said: "The Kevala [state] goes to Śambhu, who stands above Śakti, becoming absorbed in Him.
Elsewhere, the meaning regarding Viṣṇu is even clearer: "To whom Śambhu, whose abode is the lotus of His own heart..."
He who dwells in the lotus-heart of all people; the husband of Himavatī; the heart of Himavat;
the beloved of the Supreme Power (Paraśakti) as she sets forth from there; Śarva, who pierces and destroys; Rudra.
As it is said in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad:

"His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold, consisting of innate knowledge, strength, and action. Elsewhere, the meaning regarding Rudra is explicit: "I know—that is, I understand—that Tāraka, who is known by all names, beginning with Brahmā, and who possesses all designations."

Mounted upon the clouds, he is the sovereign lord of the thirty [gods]; he is the embodied bearer of fire and Time; he alone is the stainless Lord of Death, the Rākṣasa, and the dweller in the three cities;
he is the Lord of the noose and the ocean, and is declared to be the vital breath of all the worlds, the Wind.
O Three-eyed One, the Lord who has mounted his bull, your friend, stands in the northeastern quarter.

Now, Śiva—who was previously designated by names such as Viśvasṛj and so forth—is said to be one alone, yet differentiated by the designations of the guardians of the directions (*dikpāla*). He says "Megha... and so on: the one Lord (*īśa*), the supreme lord of the thirty [gods], the protector of the ten sense organs and the three internal faculties (*antaḥkaraṇa*), is described as mounted upon the cloud (*meghārūḍha*). Regarding this, there is a scriptural passage (*śruti*): "This Self..."

One worships Vaiśvānara; he is the one Lord, the stainless King of Yama. Born of the stainless Rājayoga, he is equal [to all], possessing a dark-piṅgala (tawny-black) complexion. Regarding this, there is a Śruti: "The person who is dark-piṅgala... The one Lord resides in Tripura, the sky-farer of the heart, [the source of] the sun, moon, and so forth.

He is established in the three mandalas, or else he resides in the three bodies. He is called the Rākṣasa, the protector. Regarding this, there is a scriptural passage: "The pure one, free from sorrow. He is the sole Lord, the Lord of the ocean, the leader of the heart-ocean. He is called Pāśī, the one possessing the noose of saṃsāra. Regarding this, there is a scriptural passage: (—)

By knowing the God, one is released from all bonds. He is the one Lord, the Wind (Samīra), the perfect impeller of all the senses; he is declared to be the life-breath (prāṇa) of the entire universe. Regarding this, the Śruti says: "In the heart, that light is the breath. He is the one Lord, the friend of the three-eyed [Śiva], and the New Moon, the Full Moon, and the Dark Moon.

He is the companion of the three views (*dṛṣṭitraya*). He is said to be "mounted on *nara*" (*nārārūḍha*), meaning he is the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) who mounts within the multitude of men (*narasamūha*). Regarding this, there is a scriptural citation: "Nārāyaṇa is supreme... and "Pulastya’s son is Naravāhana"; here, the suffix *aṇ* is used in its own sense (*svārthe*). He is the sole Lord (*eka īśaḥ*), the pinnacle of sovereignty (*īśānakāṣṭha*).
It is stated that one should abide in the mantra of Īśāna. Śiva alone is the one to be meditated upon; He is the maker of auspiciousness.

Having abandoned everything else, [one should remain] in the *Atharvaśikhā*. Alternatively, it may be in the mantra "Īśānaḥ sarvavidyānām" (The Lord of all sciences). According to Amara, the words *kāṣṭha* and *sthiti* mean "abiding."
Therefore, there is a Śruti passage stating that within the inner circle of those designated as world-protectors (dikpāla), there exists the Tāraka Brahman:
"They call him Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, Agni; and he is the divine, fair-winged Garuḍa. The sages speak of the One Being in many ways; they call him Viṣṇu, Yama, and Mātariśvan."

"Turāṣāṭ, Meghavāhana," and so forth; by such words of the *Amarakośa*, the meaning of the external world-protectors (*dikpāla*) is made very clear. It has not been written out here for fear of prolixity.
The Supreme Śiva, whose nature is desire, having created this web of worlds and pervaded them, has joined the multitude of moving and unmoving beings to the path of non-duality; he,
whose movement is as beautiful as the dark and white [arrows], is the performer of all actions.
If not, this triple world would likewise become devoid of all activity.
Then Śambhu, known by the previously mentioned name of the Guardian of the Quarter (Dikpāla), said "Kāma" and so forth.
"Kāma" means one whose nature is desire (*kāmātmā*); because he assumes the forms of Indra and the other gods, he is "one whose form is desire" (*kāmarūpī*).
Alternatively, he has the form of Smara (the God of Love). As it is stated in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*: "Smara indeed..."
"Greater than space is memory; therefore, even if many were to sit together, if they were not mindful, they would not hear anything at all. But if they were to reflect, then they would understand.
By means of memory one indeed recognizes one's children; by means of memory, one recognizes one's cattle. Meditate upon memory! He—

He who meditates upon Smara as Brahman— he who, as the Supreme Śiva, having created this web of worlds, the multitude of the universe, pervades that collection of worlds, [comprising] the multitude of moving and unmoving things,
the aggregate of the stationary and the wandering, and the pairs of forms such as male and female, creepers and trees, and the entire host of stationary beings.

Expanding the entire multitude of moving beings—women, men, gods, humans, animals, and so forth—she has been joined in oneness within the path of non-duality. Regarding this, the Śruti says: "Having created that, He entered into it;
from that, there came to be both the husband and the wife; whatever exists here, even down to the ants."

A woman and a man are embraced; regarding this, it was said in the *Yana-sūtra*: "While there are many archers who can split one target into two, oh, how Māra, that great archer alone, makes the two into one!"
(***) Regarding the body: it possesses the luster of black and white, yet it is stainless and white, illuminating its own locus.

Elsewhere, the meaning is clear. It is the performer of all actions—the agent of every activity, beginning with the operations of all the sense organs. On this point, the Śruti says: "Memory performs the rites dependent upon the mantras."
Likewise, were there no desire, the realm of the senses would be motionless and its functions destroyed.
That which begins with the god of love (Anaṅga) in the eight-petaled abode of passion at the *mūlādhāra*—
consisting of thirty-eight digits (*kalās*) of the sun, moon, and fire— is situated at the tip of the flame.
Through knowledge of this, both worldly enjoyment and liberation arise on this earth and beyond;
thus was the *Tāraka-pañcaratna* proclaimed by the venerable Vīraṇaguru, the best of teachers.

Now, he describes the location of Kāma and the fruit of that knowledge, beginning with the word "mūla": "The primordial bodiless Smara, residing in the eight-petaled house of Madana at the *mūlādhāra*, situated on the path of the triangle within the eight-petaled lotus of the *mūlādhāra* located in the head-lotus. Regarding this, there is a scriptural citation: "With its root above... (*ūrdhvamūlas tvam*).
The branches are speech; this is the eternal Aśvattha tree.

It has eight petals, flowers below, and a stalk above, facing downwards. Resembling the flower of the plantain tree, it is the means for attaining all the Vedas. Therein, one should contemplate the sun, the moon, and fire, each positioned higher than the last.

He who knows that which is half a *mātrā* or even less than three *mātrās* is a knower of the Veda. In the *Śivayogapradīpikā*: "In the midst of that is Fire; this is the Yoni, the triple-confluence (*triveṇī*), and this very place is the station of Yoga (*yogasthala*), the Triple Peak (*trikūṭa*)."
He who is the primordial Anaṅga, standing at the forefront of the sun, moon, and fire, which possess thirty-six and thirty-eight limited digits (*kalā*);
that is, he who stands at the head of the orbs of the sun, moon, and fire, endowed with digits measured by the number thirty-eight.
As it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa:
Tāpinī, Tāpinī, Dhūmrā, Marīci, Jvalinī, Ruci, Suṣumnā, Bhogadā, Viśvā, Bodhinī, Dhāriṇī, and Kṣamā.
The twelve digits (kalās) of the Sun are designated by pairs of syllables: Adrutā, Mānadā, Pūṣā, Tuṣi, Puṣṭi, and Ārti. Dhṛti.
Śaśinī, Candrikā, Kānti, Jyotsnā, Śrī, Prīti, Aṅgadā, Pūrṇā,
Aparṇā, and Amṛtā— these are the sixteen lunar digits (kalās) together with their vowels.
Dhūmrārcis, Ūṣmā, Jvālinī, Visphuliṅginī, Suśrī, Surūpā, Kapilā, Havyavahā, Kavyavahā,
and likewise Kalā— these are the tenfold aspects of Fire, endowed with the syllables ending at the conclusion of the sacrificial initiation (yāgadīkṣā).
Residing within the orbs of the sun, moon, and fire, he is remembered as Śiva, the primordial desire.

Through the knowledge of that Supreme Śiva—the primordial Smara—who resides within the three circles of the heart-lotus, there shall arise on earth, in this world, and in the higher realms, both enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*), which are capable of providing worldly experience and final release.
As it is said in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad: "He is the size of a thumb, with a form like the sun..."
Thus it is said. Likewise, in the *Yogasārasamuccaya*:

"In the heart-cakra, which is unstruck (*anāhata*), possesses twelve petals, and is divine light, there is in its center an eight-spoked lotus, the seat of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), facing downwards."
Within that, inside the pericarp, is a blazing form shaped like a liṅga.
Resorting to a form resembling a ruby and measuring only the size of a thumb,
there are the daughters of the Siddhas, Apsarases, Gandharvas, Nāgas, and divine women.
Men and women come under one's control at the mere thought [of this]; what wonder is there in that?
Likewise, in the *Ratirahasya*:

"The mantra of Madana consists of the final syllable of *hṛdaya* preceded by the *praṇava*, situated in the locus of space (*vyoma*) together with the wind (*sa-samīra*); it is the attractor of the left-eyed woman who is overcome by passion."

In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad: "Just as the ocean is the single goal of all waters, so the organ of generation is the single goal of all pleasures; embraced by a beloved woman, one knows nothing external nor anything internal. Thus it is said.
In the dialogue between Śiva and Rāghava:
"Of all desires, pleasure (rati) alone is the sole purpose;
all joys are gathered in one place, and pleasure resides in that very one."
"When weighed on a scale, [the latter] is a hundred times superior to pleasure," and so forth.
The details regarding worldly enjoyment have not been stated here for fear of prolixity. However, by those who are liberated, it has been said in the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad*:
"This God, the architect of the universe, the Great Soul, is eternally seated within the hearts of all people."
"Those who know this, fashioned by the heart, the mind, and the intellect, they become immortal. Likewise, in the *Śivayogapradīpikā*, there is this statement regarding the power of knowledge:
"Liberation occurs through knowledge alone within the heart. Thus, one should accept this word with reverence.
Having grasped this yoga of knowledge, become one whose mind is concentrated.
In the Śivasaṅkalpopaniṣad:
"That which is inconceivable and immeasurable, which is beyond both the manifest and the unmanifest,
and the knowledge that is subtler than the subtle— may my mind be intent upon that auspicious Śiva."
Likewise, in the *Suprabhedāgama*, it is stated in the *Śiva* [section]: "The form conjoined [with Śiva] is called *sāyujya*.
Indeed, through knowledge, there is *sāyujya* alone, just as water [merges] with water."
Likewise, in the Mānava Purāṇa:
"When supreme knowledge, which has the oneness of Brahman and the Self as its object, has arisen, supreme liberation is indeed accomplished; there is no doubt whatsoever."

And so forth; it has not been written here for fear of excessive length. This *Tāraka-pañcaratna* was proclaimed and spoken by the venerable and excellent Gurus Vīraṇa—the illustrious Sōsali Vīraṇārādhya, the sovereign among teachers.
Śrī! The commentary on the *Śrīpañcaratna* entitled *Tārakadīpikā* has been composed by the yogin Śrī Vīra(reva)ṇārādhya, disciple of Vīraṇārādhya.

[Thus ends the Tārakapradīpikā commentary on the Tārakapañcaratna, composed by Revaṇārādhya, for the work of the venerable Sosalivīraṇārādhya, who was proficient in the Veda, Vedaśiras, Śivāgama, Purāṇas, and other scriptures.]
May there be auspiciousness; salutations to Śiva. Prosperity!
This *Pañcaratnavyākhyā* was written on the tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śravaṇa in the Pārthiva year.
Salutation to Śiva.
The Elucidation of the Principle of Śiva.
Having bowed to Śiva, who is propitiated by the illustrious Vīraṇa, I compose in brief this commentary on the *Śrīpañcaratna*, which illuminates the reality of Śiva.
I bow to that which is ineffable and established as the ultimate remainder; to those two supreme Śivas who possess the form of that Liṅga;
to Śivā and Śiva who are from the very beginning of the form of that Liṅga; and to the Lord in the form of Nala, whose mantra is the recitation of that Liṅga.

Now, desiring to provide a concise commentary on this *Śivarahasyapañcaratna*, titled *Śivatatvaprakāśikā*, [the author] first states the nature of the subject matter, which is unnamed, by saying "I bow. It is established by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣasiddha*),
remaining as the object of the means of knowledge of elimination (*pariśeṣapramāṇa*), the Residual (*śiṣṭa*), the Ineffable (*anākhyam*), and that which is beyond the reach of speech and mind.

I bow to and revere the Reality (*vastu*); "I" is the understood subject. Regarding this, there is a scriptural passage (*śruti*): "From which words turn back, together with the mind, not having attained it—'not this, not this,' neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long. Likewise, in the *Mahimnaḥstava*: "[... and that greatness of yours... [The text fragment ends here].

Even the Śruti, fearing that [the Absolute] might be misconstrued as being either speech or mind, describes it by means of their exclusion. Those two, who possess the form of His signs (liṅga)—namely, the well-known supreme Śiva and Śivā, who are the very nature of the signs of that Ineffable—I bow to them.
As it is said in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad:
We know Him as the supreme Maheśvara among lords, the highest divinity among deities, the Lord beyond all lords— the adorable God, the Sovereign of the worlds.
For him there exists neither effect nor instrument; neither one equal to him nor superior to him is seen.
His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold, and his knowledge, strength, and action are innate.
Likewise, in the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā: "Let us know Him as the supreme among lords, the deity of deities, the husband of husbands, the supreme Lord of the worlds."
He has neither instrument nor effect; indeed, there is nothing equal to or superior to Him.
His manifold power is heard in the Veda as innate.
"Knowledge, action, and power—by which the universe proceeds," and so forth.
She is Śivā, who is half of that [form] whose nature is the Liṅga; and they two are Śiva and Śivā. Of those two, Paramaśivas, the two halves whose form is the Liṅga are Śivā and Śiva.
I bow to Ardhanārīśvara. As it is said in the Yajurveda: "O Rudra, your mouth..."

"O Rudra, enjoy this animal; it is your portion, together with your sister. Thus [it is said] in the *Tātparya-saṃgraha*: "O Śaṅkara, those who call her your wife in accordance with dharma are the Adhvaryu priests;
she is your sister by virtue of being innate. Such is the power of that auspicious goddess, which transcends speech and mind."
Even the Lotus-Seated One (Brahmā) is unable to describe it in its entirety. In the *Āditya Purāṇa*:
"The Lord Śiva is Ardhanārīśvara; from the female portion of Mahādeva, he created a separate Goddess. Indeed, no birth exists for her in this world..."

The gods, beginning with Brahmā, do not know him; indeed, by whose powers the multitude of cosmic eggs is pervaded. [She] was seen by Viriñci as if divided from the body. From that time forth, O best of Brahmins, progeny were born of sexual union. (From the *Laiṅga Purāṇa*)

(******) Furthermore, the cosmic eggs (*aṇḍas*) are said to be the great praises (*mahastutas*). Within each of those various [eggs], there are four-faced Brahmās, Viṣṇus, and Śivas. In all these eggs, (*****) [there are] ten [deities]. O tigers among the twice-born, Maheśvara is the cause of each individual egg. Of this [Maheśvara], there are eight forms...
In the grasping of Śarva, who is Śiva, she is the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), and from her arise the creatures beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*).

The Grandfather (*pitāmaha*) descended, having emerged like a water bubble. All beings beginning with Brahmā are his "beasts" (*paśu*), possessed of the conceit of a body. [The union] of Umā and Maheśvara is fire, water, and light in its essential form.
"Thus" means: that which has the form of fire produced from its own characteristic mark (*liṅga*). For example: "Obeisance to Hiraṇya," "Obeisance to the one whose *liṅga* is gold";
"Obeisance to Śiva," "Obeisance to the one whose *liṅga* is Śiva," and so forth. Likewise, in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"To him whose limbs are encircled by garlands of flames, who has the form of a pillar of fire..."

"Salutation to Śiva, the peaceful one, to Brahman in the form of the Liṅga," and so forth. I bow to that Rudra who is born from that Liṅga, who has arisen from that Great Liṅga. Likewise, in the *Laiṅga-purāṇa*: "Salutation to the source of the Vedas, to the flaming Liṅga, to the possessor of the Liṅga."
To the golden Liṅga and to gold, and to the water-Liṅga and to water.

"To Śiva, to the Śivaliṅga, to the Pervader, to the one who pervades space," and so forth. I bow to the supreme Śiva, known as Water and Fire, whose mother is the Gāyatrī that is not born from the Vedas and Upaniṣads; likewise [I bow] to the head of the Gāyatrī.
"Oṃ āpo jyotī raso 'mṛtaṃ brahma bhūr bhuvaḥ svaroṃ. Likewise, in the Sūtasamhitā:
"Oṃ āpo jyotiḥ"—this is the supreme head of the Gāyatrī.

Now, he describes the previously mentioned nature of Śiva’s *liṅga* with the words "tat kaṃ" (that what): "I bow to that *kaṃ*, his own formless yet multiform Great *Liṅga*. This has been stated in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad: "Salutation to the flame; salutation to the *Jvālā-liṅga*; [salutation] to Hiraṇyā..."
I bow to that Lord, the source of the marks [of the universe], whose nature is water, light, and fire.

As it is stated in the Nārāyaṇa Upaniṣad: "Water indeed is all this; water is all beings; water is the vital breaths; water is the cattle; water is food; water is immortality; water is the sovereign (samrāj); water is the universal ruler (virāj)."
The waters are self-ruling; the waters are the meters; the waters are the Yajus formulas; the waters are truth; the waters are all the deities;
the waters are *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*. In their midst is the great fire, possessing all radiance and faces in every direction.
Within the crest of that [fire] resides the Supreme Self. Thus it is stated in the *Laiṅga Purāṇa*:
Indeed, Bhūr, Bhuvas, as well as water, food, and even immortality, are breath;
for water is the life-force of the world, as are all beings and the worlds themselves.
What need is there for much speaking here? This entire world, both moving and unmoving, consists of water and Śiva; in its midst, he is established in the form of fire.
And so forth; it has not been written out here for fear of prolixity.
I bow to that Rudra born from the Liṅga— the supreme Śiva known as Nala, who is the three Vedas established solely within the head, the great Liṅga of infinite form.
Now, he reveals the previously mentioned nature of Śiva: "In water... and so forth. The triad [of Vedas] is established merely by the head [of the teacher].
As long as there is no impairment of the senses, so long worship Śaṅkara.
Life passes away swiftly; youth passes away swiftly.
Disease approaches swiftly; therefore, Sadāśiva should always be worshipped.

Likewise, in the Skanda Purāṇa: "When there is a human body, when there is the status of the twice-born, and when there is the inclination toward spiritual refinement (*paṭvīkaraṇa*), at that very time one’s own true state must be sought; for who would take back ghee once it has been spilled?"
Likewise, Bhartṛhari says:
"As long as this body is healthy and free from disease, as long as old age is far off,
as long as the power of the senses is unimpeded, and as long as there is no exhaustion of life..."
A wise person should exert great effort toward their own ultimate welfare;
for when a house is already ablaze, what kind of endeavor is it to attempt digging a well?

Furthermore, he clarifies that very meaning of the Śruti in the Ṛgveda: "O Rudra, for your glory, the Maruts soften your birth, which is beautiful and wonderful. Likewise, the Nirukta [explains]: "O Rudra, O Supreme Lord!
It is 'cāru' (beautiful), meaning exceedingly splendid; and 'citram' (wonderful), meaning worthy of being sought after (*cāyanīya*) for the sake of worship, as it is the source of the Liṅga."

He describes the true nature of Candradhara-Rudra with the word "tat": "I bow to that Rudra, born from that Great Liṅga. Likewise, in the Sāmaveda: "Salutations again and again to the one who is the highest person, the middle person, the celibate student, whose form is the moon upon his forehead and whose garment is the sky."
In the *Liṅgapurāṇa*: "That wherein the worlds dissolve and go is called the *liṅga*.
In the *liṅga*, Rudra himself, the bearer of Soma, is directly established. And so forth.
Born from that seed, the venerable atom of gold—Viṣṇu and the other gods first came into being from this;
the Vedas declare him to be the father, Hiraṇyagarbha and the rest, who is golden-hued.

Now, he describes the creation of the world from the aforementioned virility of Rudra with the word "tad" (that). "That" refers to the golden egg (*kāñcanamaṇḍa*), the egg of gold, which was born from his seed—that is, born from the fire that is the seed of Rudra, whose semen is fire. From this egg, Viṣṇu and the others first came into being. As it has been said:
In the Śivasaṃkalpopaniṣad:
In the midst [of the universe], the golden egg first came into being from the seed-power (vīrya) of Rudra within the ocean.
From the cosmic egg were born Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Agni; may my mind be of auspicious resolve.
Likewise, in the *Laiṅga*:
"The primordial syllable (akṣara), having enveloped itself, became a golden egg;

One should augment the Veda with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas.
