Having thus prostrated before the Lord, the vessel of praise for the four Vedas, he now offers salutations to the Upanishads— the crowns of the Vedas— which establish the wearing of ashes, rudrākṣa beads, the five-syllabled mantra, the wearing of the Śiva-liṅga, the sacred water from Śiva’s feet, and the grace of Śiva, beginning with the word "bhasma. Bhasma...

Regarding the *Jābāla-Ṛgveda-bhasma*, there is a scriptural passage (*śruti*) connected with the *Jābālopaniṣad* which serves as a symbolic meditation on ash; that scripture, having described the multitude of qualities of the venerable ash—the collection of glorious attributes of the sacred ash—proclaims: "It triumphs," meaning it exists in a state of supreme excellence over all worlds.
I bow to that *Jābālopaniṣad*, the lamp that illuminates the world, [and] its ashes.
As it is stated in the Ṛgveda, in the *Bhasmajābālopaniṣad*: "From meditation on the ashes, meditation on the Lord (*Īśvara*) arises;
from meditation on the ashes, the remembrance of the five-syllabled mantra (*pañcākṣarī*) arises; and from meditation on the ashes, the state of being a pillar (*sthāṇutva*) arises."

He goes [to that state]. That indeed is the light of the ashes; that indeed is the light of the ashes. By wearing the *vibhūti*, he attains oneness with Brahman. That indeed is the light of the ashes; that indeed is the light of the ashes. By wearing the *vibhūti*, the gods attain immortality. That indeed is the light of the ashes. That—

This is the light of ashes. By the mere contemplation of the ashes, one reduces sin to ashes. By the mere contemplation of the ashes, the various afflictions (*kilikiñcita*) perish. By the mere contemplation of the ashes, one effects the crossing over of *saṃsāra*. This indeed is the light of ashes; this indeed is the light of ashes. Likewise, in the Mānava Purāṇa:
"The ash indeed becomes the light known as Śiva; there is no doubt about this.
Thus and so forth, the Jābāla Upaniṣad proclaims all this with supreme joy.
Now, he speaks of the greatness of the Rudrākṣa: "That," etc. The *akṣa* [of the Jābāla] is the Rudrākṣa in the Atharvaṇa.

That triple Vedic revelation (trayī śruti) which pertains to the Jābāla Upaniṣad is the very embodiment of that rudrākṣa; thus, O rudrākṣa, having abandoned the multitude of beads and the collection of fruits of the Jābāla Upaniṣad, you alone conquer the world as the lamp of all beings.
I bow down. It has been stated in the *Rudrākṣajābālopaniṣad* of the Atharvaveda:

Then Kālāgnirudra spoke: "Regarding that Rudrākṣa which is within the sphere of speech, whatever fruit one obtains from giving ten cows when such a gift is performed, he enjoys that very fruit. 'This is the light, the Rudrākṣa,' so he said."
Desiring to touch that rudrākṣa with one's hand yields the fruit of giving a hundred cows; desiring to wear that rudrākṣa yields the fruit of giving two hundred cows;
merely by wearing that rudrākṣa, the fruit of giving a thousand cows is obtained.
When that rudrākṣa is worn on the hands, it yields the fruit of giving away two thousand cows. When that rudrākṣa is worn on the neck, it yields the fruit of giving away three thousand cows.
When worn on the ears, it yields the fruit of giving away eleven thousand cows. Eleven...
And one attains the state of Rudra. When it is worn on the head, the fruit is equal to the gift of ten million cows.
He said that the fruit for wearing these [beads] on the ears is impossible to describe. Likewise, in the Mānava Purāṇa: "Even if a person commits sin while wearing a rudrākṣa..."
"Indeed, O Jābāla, the Śruti declares that one crosses over all evil. And so forth;
it has not been written here for fear of prolixity.
Now, he describes the nature of the five-syllabled [mantra] with the words "raudra," etc.; it is the five-syllabled [mantra] of the Rudra Upaniṣad.

Having abandoned [all else], I bow to that Lamp of the worlds which conquers them; as it is stated in the *Yajurveda*’s *Śrī Rudra Upaniṣad*: "Obeisance to Śiva and to the one who is even more auspicious," and likewise in the *Śivajñānavidyā*:
Among the Vedas and the Yajus-mantras, it is established in the Śatarudriya;
because it is a Vedic utterance, it is the authoritative means for illuminating the ultimate reality.
Likewise, in the Sūta-saṃhitā: "This five-syllabled vidyā, situated within the Śatarudrīya, is purifying for all beings; it is therefore the eleven-fold Rudra."
In the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*: "One should first utter the word 'namaḥ', and after that, 'śivāya'.
This is indeed the five-syllabled mantra, which resides at the crest of all the Vedas."
"Among the seven crores of mantras, the five-syllabled mantra is the great one;
just as among Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the Rudras, Śambhu is the greatest," and so forth.
Now, he describes the wearing of the Śiva-liṅga: "But Raudrī. The word "but" (tu) indicates its distinction from what preceded.

This is illuminated by the statement of the Bhāṣya. Even the Śatarudrīya Upaniṣad, having described the birth and steadfastness of Śrī Śiva as well as the wearing of the venerable Śivaliṅga, concludes: "I bow to that lamp which triumphs over the worlds.
Likewise, in the Yajurvedic Śatarudrīya: "O Rudra, that body of yours which is auspicious, not terrible, and which does not cause sin..."

Likewise, in the Siddhāntaśiromaṇi: "Śiva, although omnipresent, is manifested more intensely in His own support, just as fire within the heartwood of a śamī tree is perceived with particular clarity."
The omnipresence of Maheśvara is established by all the scriptures;
nevertheless, there is a specific localized presence for the purpose of worship in such things as the *liṅga* and other supports.
"O Rudra, that auspicious form of yours which is non-terrible and free from the appearance of evil shines eternally among those devoted to you"— so says the eternal Śruti.
"O Rudra, that form of yours which is auspicious, non-terrible, and free from sin"—
because it is thus sung in the Yajus,
as well as in the Vedas, Shastras, Puranas, and in the Agamas such as the Kamika, [Rudra is] indeed devoid of impurity.
The wearing of the linga is declared to be the definitive characteristic of a Vīraśaiva.
Likewise, in the Śāṅkara Saṃhitā of the Skanda Purāṇa: "Whatever sin has been committed during ten million dreams, such as the killing of a Brahmin and so forth,
becomes clearly false at the time of awakening."

In the same way, whatever evil was previously committed by oneself, it goes to dissolution through the wearing of the *liṅga*; furthermore, [evil] goes to dissolution through the wearing of the *liṅga*.

The passage beginning with "pavitram" is found in the Ṛgveda; furthermore, it is stated in the Vīratantra: "Just as fragrance belongs to a flower, so does the *liṅga* belong to the body," and so forth. It has not been written out here for fear of prolixity.

Now, regarding the service of the sacred water from the feet (*pādatīrtha*) of the Śivaliṅga, [the author] says, beginning with the word *jābāla*: "Having accepted the sacred water to be served according to the Jābāla branch, and having offered the water from the feet of Śiva, I bow to that which conquers and is the lamp of the worlds. This is stated in the Jābāla branch: "Having washed the feet of the Blessed One, [one should offer it into] the conch..."
Having filled [the vessel] with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice, and other offerings, having worshipped and offered the *caru*,

and having consecrated it with the mantra "śyāmame gaṅgāyamunā," one should perform the sprinkling with the mantras "kadrudrāya" and "mā tvā rudra," and then cause [the disciple] to consume it with the mantra "ṛtaṃ satyaṃ paraṃ brahma. He who acts in this manner [purifies] those born in his lineage.

One would deliver ten ancestors and ten descendants, as well as oneself; thus says the *Abhiyukta-sūkti*: "That which begins with 'the feet of the Blessed One' exists indeed in the Jābāla recension regarding the water from the Lord's feet."
The description of the method of service is also proclaimed as his word.
Likewise, in the *Śivajñānasaṃgraha*:
"Then, having established the vessel together with water for washing the feet,
one should worship it in many ways with services such as perfumes, flowers, and so forth."
Having held that vessel upon his head while recollecting, "I am blessed," and then consecrating it with the mantra, "This is Gaṅgā and Yamunā for me."
Having grasped the hand with the mantra "kadrudrāya" and the mantra "mā tvā rudra," he should sprinkle the entire body at the sacred bathing place (tīrtha).
Then, with the entire Rudra mantra and two [additional verses], he should cause [the child] to consume it:
"Ṛta, Satya, the Supreme Brahman, the Puruṣa who is dark and tawny."
"Salutation indeed to Virūpākṣa, the one with upward-flowing vital energy, who possesses universal form"—
with these words, one should drink the remaining water from the sacred site for the attainment of knowledge and dispassion.
And in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"The lords of the Gaṇas, taking the supreme water from the feet of the Destroyer of Cities— which removes the snare of bonds—
with their hands as shells, drank it at will," and so forth.
Now, [the text] speaks of the acceptance of Śiva’s grace. In the Jābāla recension, as well as in the Jābālopaniṣad, it is said:

"Having served and accepted the grace of Śiva, one conquers; I bow to and praise that Jābālopaniṣad, which is the lamp of the worlds. Likewise, in the Jābālopaniṣad, it is stated: "They eat what has been taken by Rudra."

They drink what has been drunk by Rudra; they smell what has been smelled by Rudra. Therefore, the wise Brahmins of tranquil mind consume only the *nirmālya* (the remains of offerings). One should use only the *nirmālya*;
one should eat only the *nirmālya*. Thus it is stated in the *Siddhānta-śikhāmaṇi*:
"One should eat food eaten by Rudra, drink water drunk by Rudra,
and always smell that which has been smelled by Rudra"— such is the Jābāla Śruti.
Likewise, in the Skanda Purāṇa: "The disciplined and tranquil ones eat only what has been eaten by Rudra;
they smell only what has been smelled by him, and they drink only what has been drunk by him."
And thus runs the eloquent saying of the learned: "The wise, who know the supreme truth and whose minds are ever tranquil,
are indeed Brāhmaṇas with peaceful hearts, for they have their afflictions destroyed by Rudra."
They eat only what has been taken by Śiva; they consume only what has been consumed by him.
They drink only what has been drunk by Rudra; indeed, they smell only what has been smelled by Rudra.
They smell only the *nirmālya* and consume it with focused attention;
for that reason, it is clear that one should indeed eat only the *nirmālya*.
Such passages as "the nectar swallowed by Rudra," and so forth, which are stated in the Yajurveda, have not been written here for fear of prolixity.

The desired life-force (prāṇa) has reached the crest of the Atharva Veda; this is the definition of the Vājapeya sacrifice. This six-faced instrument is desired in the Śrī Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad and the Yājñavalkya Upaniṣads;
it consists of the nature of Tejobindu, Trayī, Haṃsa, and the Bindu and Nāda of the Niśvāsa-śiras.
I bow to that Vārāṇasī, which the crest-jewels of all the Vedas declare to be known [only] when [the Self] is realized.

Thus, having set forth the external instruction regarding the preeminence of Śiva and other matters through the two preceding verses, the author now intends to demonstrate the internal instruction concerning the *iṣṭaliṅga* and so forth by means of the following two verses.
In this verse, [the topics are] the *iṣṭaliṅga*, the *prāṇaliṅga*, the *ajapā-yoga*, the *ṣaṇmukhīkaraṇa*, the *bindu*, and the *nāda*.
Vārāṇasī succinctly demonstrates the characteristics of the liberating Brahman by stating "iṣṭam.

In the *Atharvaśiras*, that is, in the *Atharvaśira Upaniṣad*, it is "iṣṭam"—meaning it has been reached or known in the form of the desired liṅga. This is because of the statement in the *Bhāṣya*: "All verbal roots meaning 'to go' have the sense of 'to know'."
As it is said in the Atharvaśiras Upaniṣad: "Bestow upon us through austerity that which is desired and vigorous. Likewise, in the Vātula Tantra:
"The entire great site of the chosen *liṅga* is to be grasped by the faculty of sight."
It directly brings about the attainment of what is desired and the avoidance of what is undesired.
He always bestows desired vigor upon his own devotees.
Therefore, the Atharvaṇa Śruti declares that the Liṅga is the desired object of worship.
Likewise, in the Sūtagītā:
"The form characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss is like the solidity of clarified butter;
it does not exist as distinct from Śiva, for it is always Śiva himself," and so forth.
Now, he describes the nature of the *prāṇaliṅga*, which is the very life-force (*prāṇabhūta*) of the unmanifest *liṅga* (the *atheṣṭaliṅga*), by saying "the *prāṇa*.

The *prāṇa*, that is, the *prāṇaliṅga* as well, is "gone to"—meaning known—precisely in the *Atharvaśrutiśiras*, i.e., in the *Atharvaśira Upaniṣad*. According to the *Viśva* lexicon: "The particle *vā* is used in the sense of option, comparison, the word 'only' (*evārtha*), and conjunction (*samuccaya*)."
Likewise, in the *Atharvaśiras Upaniṣad* it is said: "They call the mark (liṅga) that which is within the vital breaths and the mind.
Similarly, in the *Vātula Tantra*:
"The Prāṇaliṅga is to be grasped by the mind; it is both with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala)."
"The Śruti declares that the mark of the mind is within those very vital breaths."

Likewise, in the *Āditya Purāṇa*: "They say that within the vital breaths (prāṇas) is the mark of the mind, in which there is anger, thirst, and forbearance. Having cut through thirst—the root of the snare-net—and having reflected with the intellect, one should then establish [the mind] in Rudra," and so forth. It has not been written out in full for fear of prolixity.

Then he spoke regarding Ajapā: "Śrī" means the definition of Ajapā, the nature of the Ajapā-yoga, which is found in the venerable *Īśāvāsya-śruti*, that is, it occurs in the *Śrīmad-Īśāvāsya Upaniṣad*.
As it is stated in the *Īśāvāsya Upaniṣad*: "That which is the Sun, that person; I am He."
Likewise, in the Sūta-saṃhitā:
"Now, this mantra 'Atha aham' (Then, I am) establishes the individual self (jīvātman);
the Śakti-mantra known as the letter 'Sa' denotes the Supreme Lord."
The Supreme Lord is well-known because he is established in the subject matter at hand.
I am an entity existing within saṃsāra; that very one is the Supreme Lord. I am indeed He, without a doubt, according to the authority of my own direct experience.
The Śruti also speaks in this very way, revealing the ultimate truth:
"Following the scriptures and guided by reason under the direction of a teacher, the wise man should realize: 'I am He; He indeed is I.'"
In the Haṃsa Upaniṣad: "Haṃsa, haṃsa"—thus [the Self] always exists pervading all bodies.
Just as fire is in wood or oil in sesame seeds, having known that, one does not go to death.
Now, the seer is Haṃsa, the meter is Gāyatrī unmanifest, and the deity is Paramahaṃsa. Six.
The number of days and nights [in a kalpa] amounts to twenty-one thousand six hundred. Likewise, in the Vivekamārtaṇḍa:
"By the letter *sa*, the breath goes out; by the letter *ha*, it enters."
The individual soul always recites that mantra, "Haṃsa, haṃsa."
Six hundred and twenty-one thousand [repetitions] of the Gāyatrī, known as Ajapā, bestow liberation upon yogis day and night.
By the mere resolve of this [goddess], a man is liberated from sins.
Likewise, in the Yoga-bīja,
the vital breath (marut) goes out with the letter *sa* and enters with the letter *ha*;
this mantra "haṃsa, haṃsa" is that which all living beings recite.
Through the word of the Guru, the recitation within the suṣumnā becomes reversed;
when the realization "I am He, I am He" is attained, that is called mantra-yoga.
And realization arises through the application of mantra on the Western Path.
Likewise, in the *Śivayogapradīpikā*: "This seed-syllable ending in *sa*, accompanied by the nasal drop (*bindu*), goes outward;
this seed-syllable ending in *ṣa*, accompanied by the visarga, enters within."
By resolving upon what is called the ajapā [mantra], a person is liberated from sins.
"One attains the yoga of Śiva very quickly; of this there is no doubt," and so forth. Now, the performance of the Ṣaṇmukhī mudrā is described in the Yājñavalkya-śruti;
it has been understood as having reached the point of praise in the Yājñavalkyopaniṣad. Thus, in the Yājñavalkyopaniṣad—
Having taken his seat, the wise one, with a concentrated mind, should likewise bring the organs under control by force from their objects.
Having drawn the apāna upward with the praṇava while remaining composed,
one should properly bind the sense organs, beginning with the ears, using both hands.
Having covered both ears with the two thumbs, the two eyes with the two index fingers, and the nostrils and the sense organs with the remaining fingers;
One should hold [the breath] at the crown of the head for as long as bliss (ānanda) manifests;
otherwise, the vital breath (prāṇa) departs by that very means, thereby causing the destruction of one's lifespan.
In the Brahma-randhra, within the Suṣumṇā like a thread inside a lotus stalk, the arising of the Nāda occurs;
it is indeed like pure crystal.
The sound (nāda) exists at the head, rising like the neck of a lute;
it is like the sound of a conch at first, and like the roar of clouds in the middle.
When the sound has entered the aperture of space, it is like a mountain stream;
when the wind has entered the aperture of space and the mind is established in its own self.
In that way, the embodied being becomes joyful, and by that, the vital air (vāyu) is conquered.
Likewise, in the Siddhāntaśekhara: "Having assumed the vajrāsana, one should bind the ears and so forth as follows:
both ears with the two thumbs, and the eyes with the two index fingers."
One should firmly bind the pair of nostrils with the two middle fingers;
this is indeed the "six-faced" (ṣaṇmukhī) technique, which is praised for the arising of the internal sound (nāda).

Likewise, in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad: "One should practice meditation in a cave sheltered from the wind, which is favorable to the mind and not distressing to the eyes. These forms—mist, smoke, sun, water, fire, a firefly, lightning, crystal, and the moon—are the precursors to Brahman."
The individual means [of practice] are in Yoga. Likewise, in the *Śivayogapradīpikā*:

"Having filled the mouth with air, having drawn up the *apāna* into the abode of fire (*hutavaha*), and having held it by blocking the six fingers—the thumbs and so forth—of both hands with the palms."
Through this path, the wise— whose minds are absorbed in the various sounds accompanied by the *praṇava*— behold signs within the ears, the eyes, and the pair of nostrils.

And so forth; it has not been written here for fear of prolixity. Now he states the definition of the *bindu*: "The Radiance" (*tejaḥ*). The triad of *bindus* is in the head; the nature of the *bindu* is known from the *Tejobindu Upaniṣad*.
Likewise, in the *Atharvaṇa*, in the *Tejobindu Upaniṣad*:
The supreme meditation on the *tejobindu* abides in the heart, transcending the universe;
it is that which is atomic (*āṇava*), originating from Śambhu (*śāmbhava*), and arising from power (*śākta*), as well as that which is gross, subtle, and supreme.
Likewise, in the *Niśvāsakārikā*:
"Having the form of a mass of smoke or clouds, extensive and facing in all directions,
it is seen and then vanishes, with a brilliance like that of a firefly."
The middle dot is said to resemble the saffron of Hari.
Situated in the middle of the eye, it blazes and is filled by its own radiance.
The Bindu, resembling pure crystal, should be known as higher than the highest;
it consists of the ten deities and bestows the fruits of the ten actions.
And one should understand the ten forms, which are subtler than the subtle and supreme:
white, red, black, blue, with the luster of a cloud,
yellow, crimson, pale yellow, tawny, and smoky.
The tenth is like crystal; their respective fruits are as follows:
white for the purpose of subduing, and red for the destruction of spirits.
For the destruction of Piśācas, Kṛṣṇa was taught by the high-souled Śiva;
for the destruction of all seizing spirits (grahas), Nīla is indeed proclaimed.
Cloud-colored [smoke] is for the destruction of disease; yellowish-red for killing;
yellow for attraction; and smoke that is tawny is prescribed for killing.
One with a very smoky luster accomplishes all actions, while one with the luster of crystal bestows liberation;
these are, respectively, the presiding deities of all the drops, beginning with the white and so forth.
Ananteśa and the others are proclaimed as the principal [forms], ending with Śikhaṇḍin;
Kālāgnirudra is the ninth, while Sadāśiva is the tenth.
"This is the primary characteristic of the deity Bindu, known as Śiva.

By constant meditation on the Bindu, the yogi shall attain the perfection of yoga," and so forth. Now, he describes the nature of Nāda with the word "Haṃsa": in the *Haṃsopaniṣad*, which is at the head of the Vedas (the *Haṃsanigama*), [it speaks of] Nāda.

The true nature [of the Self] has been known. Thus, in the Haṃsa Upaniṣad: "This very Paramahaṃsa is like ten million suns; by ten million recitations of this [mantra], the Nāda (the primordial sound) becomes manifest. And that arises in ten forms:
'ciṇ' is the first, 'ṇic' is the second, and the resonance of a bell is the third."

The fourth is the sound of the conch; the fifth is the sound of the lute; the sixth is the sound of the cymbals; the seventh is the sound of the flute; the eighth is the sound of the kettledrum; the ninth is the sound of the mṛdaṅga drum; the tenth is the sound of the clouds. Having abandoned the ninth, one should practice the tenth alone. When the mind has dissolved into that [sound], in the mind—
When conceptualization and doubt have departed and merit and sin are burnt away, there is eternal Śiva.
Thus, in the world of Śiva, there is the sound *ciṇ-ciṇ-ciṇ*. Furthermore, there are the sounds of bells, conchs, and the resonance of lutes;
amidst the cries of "Sattā," the sounds of kettledrums and clay drums arise—these are the ten sounds proclaimed in the Siddhāntaśekhara.
Through this practice of nāda, the powers beginning with aṇimā arise,
as well as various other accomplishments such as hearing and seeing from a distance.
Such details have not been written here for fear of prolixity.
Having thus described the six-faced [mantra] consisting of the desired vital breaths (*prāṇa*), the recitations (*japa*), and the nature of the *bindu* and *nāda*,
what follows is the *Gāyatrī-śiras*, which is well-known as the crown of all the Vedas and is to be understood through the instruction of the Guru.

It demonstrates the knowledge of the Supreme Self: "All" (*sakala*). "All the crests of the Vedas" (*sakala-śruti-śikhāḥ*) refers to all the summits of the Vedas, such as the *Kṣetrajña* and *Jābāla Upaniṣads*. Regarding the word "that" (*tat*), the commentary states that it is well-known, referring to a subject already introduced or commonly experienced; such a pronoun does not require the prior mention of a relative pronoun (*yat*).

Because of this statement: Vārāṇasī is the field of non-liberation (Avimuktakṣetra). That which is Vārāṇasī, they call the Tāraka Brahman, whose nature is the established Supreme Self. That I bow to and revere.
This has been stated in the Kṣetrajābāla Upaniṣad: "Then Atri questioned Yājñavalkya... [and so on].
"How may I know this unmanifest Self? Yājñavalkya replied:
"That which is infinite and unmanifest, that Self is to be meditated upon as the Unliberated (Avimukta); it is established in the Unliberated.
[The question was asked: "In what is that Unliberated established? [The answer was: "In the middle of the Varaṇā and the Nāśī."

Regarding the term "established" (*pratiṣṭhita*): what is *varaṇā* and what is *nāśī*? It wards off (*vārayati*) all defects produced by the senses; therefore it is *varaṇā*. It destroys (*nāśayati*) all evils produced by the senses;
therefore it is *nāśī*. And how does its path of entry come to be? That which [lies] between the two eyebrows and the nose.

"This junction is the junction of the heavenly world with the beyond; that is the Avimukta, which is to be meditated upon. For here, when the vital breaths of a living being are departing, Rudra reveals the liberating Brahman, by which he becomes immortal and attains liberation. Thus it is stated in the Sūtasamhitā.
O one of great wisdom, Vārāṇasī is in the middle between the eyebrows and the nose;
"the junction of the eyebrows and the nose"—such is the Jābāla Śruti.
Likewise, in the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, Śiva says: "That place which wards off all sins and destroys them in an instant is Vārāṇasī; the wise know it to be between the two eyebrows."
O Noble Lady, you alone are the light of the Linga, and I am the possessor of the Linga, Maheśvara.
Therefore, O beloved, behold this very light known as Avimukta.
Likewise, in the world of Śiva, there is indeed the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā rivers; yet there is a certain wondrous reality in Avimukta:
that light which is the self of the Liṅga and the self of the Savior—that very light, O Lord, I behold as You.
In the sacred field of Avimukta, Rudra, having abandoned his sons, proclaimed the Tāraka Brahman in the right ear; one becomes liberated thereby, and not otherwise.
Likewise, in the Mānava Purāṇa: "The junction between the eyebrows and the nose is where Vārāṇasī is situated;
there lies the sacred field of Avimukta, and in it Rudra is eternally present."
The Liṅga, known as Viśveśvara, is eternally of the nature of light;
it is the direct deliverer from saṃsāra and should be worshipped for the sake of liberation.
Likewise, in the Śaṅkarasaṃhitā:
"In the region of Avimukta, situated between the eyebrows, there is the supreme self-liṅga known as Viśveśvara;
having meditated upon it, great souls whose minds are attached to the nectar of meditation attained supreme liberation."
Such details have not been written here for fear of prolixity. Now, that which is situated in the field of Avimukta, endowed with names such as Agni and others,
possessing the nature of the Supreme Self, is the Tāraka Brahman, which is present even in all the Vedāntas, the Gāyatrī, and the Śiras-mantras.

He demonstrates [this]: in the glorious Ṛgveda—*Oṃ, I praise Agni, the domestic priest* (1); in the Yajurveda—*Salutation to Agni accompanied by the waters* (2); in the Sāmaveda—*Salutation to Agni, the dweller in the earthly world* (3);
in the Atharvaśiras—*He who is indeed Rudra is the Blessed One, and he who is Agni; to him indeed, salutation after salutation* (4).
In the Śivasankalpopaniṣad: "He who knows [this] protects all the worlds from the waters, the Great Lord; through the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas, may my mind be of auspicious resolve. (1)
In the Śrī Rudra Upaniṣad: Salutations to Tāra and salutations to Śambhu. 2.

In the Atharvaśira Upaniṣad: Now, why is it called "Tāra"? Because, as soon as it is uttered, it carries one across the great fear of the cycle of existence consisting of birth from the womb, old age, and death; therefore, it is called "Tāra. (3)
In the Brahmavidyopaniṣad, that which stands above the Praṇava is to be known as having half a mora (ardhamātrā). ||4||
In the Dhyānabindu Upaniṣad: "He who knows that which is half a mora or even a quarter-mora [beyond] the three moras—he is a knower of the Veda. (5)

In the Haṃsa Upaniṣad: "I am the one with three measures (trimātra)"—thus one should always meditate. (6) In the Kaṭha Upaniṣad: "The Person is the size of a thumb. (7) In the Prāṇāgnihotra Upaniṣad: "This very person is indeed great, who is established on the tip of the thumb. (8) In the Brahma Upaniṣad: "The one God..."
Hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner self of all beings. 10.

In the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad: "The Person, the size of a thumb, is the inner self, eternally seated in the heart of all people. (9) In the Amṛtabindu Upaniṣad: "The Self alone is to be meditated upon. (11)
In the Mahopaniṣad: "The Puruṣa is the Supreme Self. (12) In the Muṇḍakopaniṣad: "For the divine, formless Puruṣa... (13) In the Pūrvatāpanīyopaniṣad: "The Puruṣa alone is all this. (14)
In the *Uttaratāpanīyopaniṣad*: "For all this is Brahman; this Self is Brahman. (15)

In the Vṛddhajābāla Upaniṣad: "The Supreme Self is the witness of all actions. (16) In the Praśna Upaniṣad: "The person is the self of consciousness. (17) In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad: "The person is the light within the heart;
he is this self, to be realized as 'not this, not this'. (18) In the Āśvalāyana Upaniṣad: "Indeed, he is here in the heart..."
The Puruṣa-sūkta: "The Person. (19) In the Taittirīya Upaniṣad: "Bliss is the Self. (20) In the Paramahaṃsa Upaniṣad:
"That which is the singular consciousness of perfect bliss—that is Brahman. (21) In the Maṇḍala Brāhmaṇa Upaniṣad:
"Brahman alone is this universe, this most excellent. (22) In the Jābāla Upaniṣad: "That is Brahman. (23)
That should be worshipped. (23) In the Nārāyaṇa Upaniṣad: "The Truth, the Reality, the Supreme Brahman, the Person, dark and tawny... (24)
In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "This person who is seen within the eye—this is the Self. (26)
In the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad: "That Self is to be known. In the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa Upaniṣad:

"This very person who is in the waters—that is the Brahman I venerate. This very person who is in the mirror—that is the Brahman I venerate. (27) In the Aitareya Upaniṣad: "They venerate the heart..."

The Aruṇas [declare] "Brahman"; the deities are Brahman. (28) In the *Tejobindu Upaniṣad*: "This supreme, secret place is the manifest Brahman, which is without support. (29) In the *Yājñavalkya Upaniṣad*: "Also in the middle of the heart, on the forehead, [is] the pillar... (sthāṇu)
The linga is invisible. (30) In the Yajurveda Upanishad:
"That which is this space within the heart—within it is this person consisting of mind, consisting of immortality, and golden."

31. Having thus known the form of the Supreme Self—which dwells in the cave of the heart, is partless and non-dual, the witness of all, devoid of being and non-being—one attains the pure form of the Supreme Self. (From the *Kaivalyopaniṣad*. In the *Amṛtanādopaniṣad* of the venerable Ṛgveda, [the mantra] with the *Vyāhṛtis*... sa...

One should recite the Praṇava along with the Gāyatrī and its Śiras three times while holding the breath; that is called Prāṇāyāma. (Yajurveda Nārāyaṇopaniṣad): I invoke Gāyatrī; I invoke Sāvitrī; I invoke Sarasvatī. Oṃ Bhūḥ, Oṃ Bhuvaḥ, Oṃ Svaḥ, Oṃ.

Mahas Om, Janas Om, Tapas Om, Satyam Om. Om! We meditate upon that most excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ; may he impel our intellects. Om! Water, light, essence, immortality, Brahman, Bhūr, Bhuvas, Svar, Om. In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad of the Sāmaveda, Speech indeed makes known the Ṛgveda and the Yajurveda.

The Sāmaveda, the Atharvaveda as the fourth, and the Itihāsa-Purāṇa as the fifth Veda among the Vedas—verily, all this existing world is speech; it sings and protects. That which is indeed Gāyatrī is this very speech. ||3||

In the *Atharvaśikhopaniṣad*, having spoken thus three times, the fourth is the peaceful Self; by means of the protracted pronunciation (*pluta*), the entire "Om" is employed as the light of the Self. In the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad*:
This should be known as eternally established in the Self; indeed, there is nothing further than this to be known.
In the heart-lotus, the size of a thumb, at the summit of the orbs of the sun,

moon, and fire, there is a blazing radiance— the nature of water and light— situated in the cavity of the *yama* (the central channel), hidden within all beings; it is the direct object of perception within, pervading the entire universe, and possesses the splendor of lightning amidst the clouds.
I bow to that subtle Brahman, the nectar of immortality, which transcends darkness and is of the nature of knowledge.

Now, in this verse, the meaning of the Gāyatrī—the crown jewel of all the scriptures written in the preceding verses, the thirty-two Upaniṣads which are the head of the four Vedas, and the mother of those [Upaniṣads]—is gradually revealed somewhat: "In the lotus of the heart. This is from the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.
"The heart is indeed Brahman; the heart is indeed Brahman. "What would there be for one without a heart?
"The heart, O Sovereign, is the supreme Brahman; it does not abandon him. Likewise, in the world of Śiva, this heart-cakra is stainless and adorned with seven circles.
It is joined with the three mandalas and likewise consists of the nature of the sun, moon, and fire.
Likewise, in the Skanda-purāṇa:
"Salutation to that Mahādeva, whose splendor, having pierced through the seven coverings, shines forth externally while residing within the heart," and so forth.

"Of the size of a thumb," as stated in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad: "The Person of the size of a thumb, the inner self, is eternally seated in the hearts of all people. Likewise, in the Pauṣkara: "In the world of the size of a thumb, liberation (kaivalya) may be attained by the bound soul (paśu). Similarly, [in the teachings of] Śaṅkara...
In another [portion of the] Saṃhitā,

it is said that in ancient times, noble sages attained liberation by meditating upon Śiva— the immeasurable, primordial Liṅga whose nature is consciousness— as blazing within the lotus of the heart, the size of a thumb.
And so forth. Regarding the phrase "the tip of the orb of the sun, moon, and fire is blazing," the *Dhyānabindu Upaniṣad* states:
"Below is an eight-petaled lotus with its stalk above and facing downward."
Resembling the flower of the plantain tree, it brings about the attainment of all the Vedas.
Therein, one should contemplate the sun, the moon, and the fire, each situated above the other;
he who knows this, whether for three measures or even half a measure, is a knower of the Veda.

Likewise, in the *Śivayogapradīpikā*: "He who, through the grace of the Guru, having destroyed the three impurities and having known that Śiva— who is of the nature of pure consciousness and resides within the orbs of the sun, moon, and fire— worships Him, attains the bliss of liberation."

Likewise, in the Mahābhārata: "Having meditated upon the lotus of the heart situated within, with its stalk pointing upward and its face downward—[then one should visualize it] as having eight petals and pericarp, with its face turned upward and fully blossomed."
One should place the Sun, Moon, and Fire upon the pericarp (karṇikā), and in its center, one should contemplate the form of Śiva, the supreme meditation. Thus it is said, and so forth.
"Water, light, and the nature of sound"—as stated in the *Prāṇāgnihotra Upaniṣad*: "Water, light, food, and immortality; water..."
May the earth purify [us], and may the earth, being purified, purify me. Likewise, in the *Śivayogapradīpikā*:
"Just as the wise behold the form of light, which is the immortal Brahman, whose nature is Śiva—that wearyless, supreme abode of Viṣṇu."
Likewise, in the *Āditya Purāṇa*: "They know the Supreme Lord as residing in the waters...
and whose very form is water; salutations to that Supreme Self," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "gone to the cavity of the throat" (*vamī kuhara-gatam*), the meaning is that he is known by yogis within the cave of the heart.
In the *Yājñavalkyopaniṣad*: "Smaller than the smallest and greater than the greatest, the Self is hidden in the cave of this living being;
one who is free from sorrow beholds that wonder even at the time of death with a purified intellect.
Likewise, in the *Yogasārasaṃgraha*: "In the center of the cavity of the heart, like a lamp, is the essence of the Vedas..."

He who meditates even once with his mind upon that which consists of the *praṇava*, which is inconceivable, accessible through the meditation of yogis, the union of Hari, Guru, and Śiva, the one abiding in all beings— he is liberated. Thus, in the *Śivarāghava-saṃvāda*:
In the center of the heart-lotus there is a cavity, and therein indeed are the five elements;
in the center of that is the great space, and within that pure space is the reed.
"And in the midst of that, one should meditate upon Maheśāna, Śiva, who consists of light," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "hidden in all beings," the *Brahmopaniṣad* states:
"The one God is hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner self of all beings."
The overseer of karma, the abode of all beings, the witness, the conscious one, solitary and devoid of qualities.

In the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad*: "Having known Śiva, who is subtler than the cream on the surface of clarified butter, hidden within all beings, the one who envelops the universe—having known that God, one is released from all bonds. Likewise, in the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā*:
"Having known Śiva as the subtle presiding Lord, who is like the cream atop clarified butter, hidden within all beings, one is liberated from all bonds"—and so forth.

Regarding the term "direct perception" (*pratyakṣam*): it is direct perception in each and every eye (*akṣiṇyakṣiṇi*). It has its mark within; that is, it consists of the internal mark (*antarlakṣātmakam*).

In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad: "The eye, indeed, is Brahman; the eye, indeed, is Brahman. For what would happen to one who does not see? "The eye, O Emperor, is the supreme Brahman. The eye does not desert him. Likewise, in the perception of the moon: 'The light of the Self, the light of the mind—the light of the eye does not see.'"
That light which is both external and internal is called Śiva. Thus, in the *Sūtasaṃhitā*:

"One should perceive Śiva through the instruction of the Guru; one should also perceive Śiva by means of that perception. Having even abandoned that perception, only one's own consciousness remains as its true, innate nature."
And so forth. "Going to all worlds" means pervading the universe.

In the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad: "Having known Śiva—the creator of the universe, who is subtler than the subtle, who exists in the midst of the waters, who possesses manifold forms, and who alone encompasses the universe—"

One attains ultimate peace. And so it is said in the *Candrāvalokana*: "Just as a gem [reflects] that which is constantly shimmering before the eyes, by beholding that all-pervading Śambhu, one is liberated from the bonds of existence."
Likewise, in the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā: "The Lord, who is subtler than the subtlest, who dwells even in the midst of the waters,
who is the creator of the universe and its enveloper."

"Having known Śiva alone as the Lord, one attains ultimate peace," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "having the luster of lightning in a cloud": in the *Nārāyaṇopaniṣad* it is said, "The heart is like the interior of a lotus bud, and it is downward-facing."
At its end is a subtle cavity; in that, everything is established.
In its center is a great fire, possessing all radiance and faces in every direction;
in the middle of that is the crest of the flame, situated as something exceedingly subtle and upward-pointing.
Resplendent like a streak of lightning situated in the midst of a dark blue cloud,
she is slender like the awn of wild rice, golden-hued, and radiant as the sun.
In the center of that crest-lock, the Supreme Self is established.
In the Yājñavalkya Upaniṣad:
Resplendent like a streak of lightning in the midst of a dark blue cloud,
having the form of the awn of a grain of wild rice, golden-hued, it is the cause of all.
Likewise, in the Sūta-saṃhitā:
"One should meditate on [the form] which is situated in the midst of a dark blue cloud, radiant like a streak of lightning,
having the appearance of the awn of a wild grain (nīvāra), and possessing a yellowish luster," and so forth.

Regarding "subtle": In the *Yājñavalkyopaniṣad*, it is stated: "That form which is in the sky within the heart-lotus—truthful, eternally blissful, and most subtle—that Brahman, consisting of radiance, is in the cave. And the *Śruti* also records this in the same way. Likewise, in the *Vātula*:
One should contemplate its true nature as a subtle form, a form of light,
manifest everywhere like lightning in the sky.
Likewise, in the *Śivarāghava-saṃvāda*: "One should perceive Śiva, who resides at the tip of the twelve-finger space [of the head],
subtle in form, moving within all beings, in the cave of the heart, and in all universal forms."
"Having meditated upon that, one should hold it in the mind and fill the body with its radiance," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "the nectar of Brahman": in the *Brahmavidyopaniṣad*, it is said: "That in which sound dissolves is sung as the True Brahman;
he who contemplates that eternal Brahman is fit for immortality—he is fit for immortality."
It is prescribed: "Oṃ āpo jyotī raso 'mṛtaṃ brahma bhūr bhuvaḥ svar oṃ" as the head of the Gāyatrī.
Likewise, in the Sūtasamhitā: "Oṃ āpo jyotiḥ"—this is the supreme head of the Gāyatrī.

And so forth. "Beyond the darkness" refers to the Kaivalya Upaniṣad: "Having meditated upon the stainless and pure lotus of the heart, in its center [one perceives] the luminous, sorrowless, inconceivable, unmanifest, infinite-formed, auspicious, tranquil, immortal Brahman, the source; that which is devoid of beginning, middle, and end, the one, the all-pervading."
Having meditated upon that wonderful, formless Consciousness-Blessedness, which is the source of all beings and the witness of all, beyond darkness, the sage goes [to liberation].
(Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad) — "I know this Great Person, resplendent like the sun, beyond darkness; knowing Him thus, one transcends death."
"No other path exists for liberation. Likewise, in the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā:

"I know this great Puruṣa, immortal and eternal, resplendent like the sun, situated beyond darkness, the Lord," and so forth. "Consisting of the nature of knowledge" refers to the knowledge of the Tāraka-Brahman.
I bow to and praise Him, that Supreme Śiva, whose essential nature is such:
"That which is inconceivable and immeasurable, both manifest and unmanifest, and supreme;
the knowledge subtler than the subtle—may my mind be intent upon Śiva. (Śivasankalpopaniṣad)

In the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad: "This God, the Architect of All, the Great Soul, is eternally seated in the hearts of all people. Those who know Him, through the heart, through intuition, and through the mind, become immortal. Likewise, in the Śivayogapradīpikā: "Liberation arises from knowledge alone within the heart."
Having respectfully accepted this statement, become one whose mind is concentrated on this yoga of knowledge.
In the *Suprabhedāgama*, it is stated in the *Śiva* [section] that the form joined [with the deity] is called "union" (*sāyujya*).
Indeed, through knowledge, union occurs in this very way, just as [water merges] with water.
Likewise, in the Mānava Purāṇa:
"When supreme knowledge, which has the oneness of Brahman and the Self as its object, has arisen, supreme liberation is indeed accomplished; there is no doubt whatsoever."

Such details have not been written here for fear of excessive prolixity. My commentary on this *Śrutisārapañcaratna*, titled *Upadeśaśiromaṇi*, is merely a compendium; therein everything should be understood through the instruction of the preeminent teacher. 4.

In the lineage of the illustrious Reṇuka was born Vāraṇāsīśvara, an abode of immeasurable sacred learning; his son was Sarveśa, whose name was honored by Śiva and Yama; and his son composed this entire [work], which is endowed with all the scriptures, unassailable by any mortals, and to be taught by all teachers.
The Five Jewels, which are like the crest-jewels of the Vedas.

Then the eminent teacher named Vīraṇārādhya, who is worthy of being honored by the world, spoke of the lineage of his own family and the greatness of his own composition, the *Śrutisārapañcaratna*, a hymn to Śiva—
beginning with the words "In the lineage": "In the lineage of the venerable Reṇuka, [there was] the illustrious teacher Revanāsiddheśa."

He was a sovereign ruler, himself an abode of immeasurable learning, proficient in all the scriptures, and the lord of Vārāṇasī. He became the preeminent elephant among teachers, known by the name Ācārya Deva, renowned in the city of Uttaravārāṇasī. As it is stated in the *Dīkṣāvidhāna*: "Always [acting] in the performance of the rite..."
In the Śivācārya lineage there was Eka-varṇaka; in the Dvāpara age, Reṇukācārya; and in the Kali age, the one named Śrī Revana.

Therefore, by me, named Śrīmad-Revaṇārādhya— the son of the illustrious Revaṇāsiddheśvara, who is like the full moon nourishing the ocean of his lineage, and who follows the sequence of elders in the hereditary succession of the venerable Revaṇāsiddha, the sovereign preceptor— [this work is composed].

It is stated in the *Śrīmad-upadeśa-śiromaṇi*: "The son of the Lord of Vārāṇasī, who is the banner of Revanasiddha—the source of the stainless lineage and the master of all accomplishments—was Yamindra, the son of Sunayatanaya Sarveśa; he was proficient in all arts and was known as Sosalī Vīraṇa."

This genealogical succession is well-known throughout all the world. Thus it was stated by the venerable Girīndra in his commentary on the *Ekottara-śata* (the "One Hundred and One"): "There exists, the bestower of welfare upon the earth, a form of Śiva-consciousness; O Lord, it is named Vārāṇasī."
"Expert in all philosophical systems (pāragaḥ). Regarding the word "all": he was the son of that Lord of Vārāṇasī;

his abode was Śivayamana, and he took refuge in the yoga of Śiva. Being the manifest Lord of All (sarveśaḥ), he became the preeminent teacher Sarveśvarācārya at Śrīsosalī, near the Śmaśānakūṭa in Vārāṇasī.
This has been stated by the venerable Vīraṇārādhya in the *Śrutisāraprakāśikā*:

"Salutations to the Lord of All, who was born in Vārāṇasī and dwells within the lotus-abode amidst the multitude of the illustrious lords of yogins. [Regarding] "his son": he was the son of that sovereign teacher of all masters (sarveśvarācārya-sārvabhauma).

The preceptor named Vīraṇārādhya, known as Śrīmatsosali Vīraṇārādhya, became the sovereign of all teachers. As it has been said by Basavadeva himself at the beginning and end of his *Svātmayogapradīpikā* with its commentary: [...]* *Note: The ellipsis indicates the omission of the specific verses from the cited source.*
I salute the Guru, the Lord of the Universe, who has taken refuge in the supreme state of being,
the excellent knower of reality, wandering among ascetics on the paths of the Vedas.
"Salutations to the glorious Guru Vīreśa, who shines as the embodiment [of the deity];
salutations to you, the Supreme Self, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss. Such passages have not been written here for fear of prolixity;
the account of this lineage should be learned from those who are experts in it.

Now he describes the greatness of this Five Jewels (*pañcaratna*): "akhila... and so forth. "Akhila" means accompanied by all that has been heard—that is, joined with the entire collection of scriptures such as the Vedas, Vedāntas, Āgamas, Purāṇas, Itihāsas, and so on.
As it is said in the Nārāyaṇopaniṣad: "The Lord of all sciences, the Sovereign."
Regarding the phrase "of all beings": likewise, in the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā it is said:
"The four Vedas, Mīmāṃsā, the expansion of Nyāya, the Purāṇa, and the Dharmaśāstra—these indeed are the fourteen branches of knowledge."
Āyurveda, Dhanurveda, and Gāndharvaveda follow in that order.
Including another treatise on statecraft (arthaśāstra), these are indeed remembered as the eighteen branches of knowledge.
The sacred tradition declares that the wielder of the trident (Śūlapāṇi) is the manifest primordial author of these eighteen branches of knowledge, which follow diverse paths.

And so forth. For this very reason, he states that all the statements of the entire body of scriptures—beginning with the Vedas and Upaniṣads—promulgated by Śiva are inviolable for all mortals; furthermore, the words of the elders who follow those [scriptural] statements must not be transgressed. Thus says Śiva in the Skanda Purāṇa:
One must not transgress the words of these great sayings of the Śruti and Smṛti;
he who violates my command is a traitor to me and is born in the womb of a dog.
The Vedas are authoritative; the Smṛtis are authoritative; words consistent with dharma and worldly purpose are authoritative.
For one who does not accept what is authoritative as authoritative, who would accept his word as authoritative?
He for whom the Vedas, the Śaiva scriptures, and the words of the elders do not constitute authority—
that evil-souled man, struck down by the sins prescribed for him, possesses no authority even regarding his own self in this world.

And so forth. Now, he states that the secret knowledge of this *Śrutisārapañcaratna* is not known by anyone at all without the instruction of an elephant among teachers (*deśika-kuñjara*), using the words "by the teachers" (*ācāryaiḥ*).
This refers to those designated by the word "teacher" (*ācārya*), namely the tigers among instructors (*deśika-śārdūla*), who are to provide the instruction. As it has been said in the *Siddhānta*:

In the *Śiromaṇi*: "Because he gathers (*ācinoti*) the meanings of the scriptures and firmly establishes them in right conduct (*ācāra*), and because he practices them himself, he is therefore called an *ācārya*. In the *Yajurvedopaniṣad*: "The teacher (*ācārya*) is the prior form; the disciple (*antevāsin*) is the subsequent form; knowledge (*vidyā*) is the junction (*sandhi*). In the *Īśāvāsyopaniṣad*: "For the sake of understanding that [Self], he..."
One should approach a Guru alone—possessing Vedic learning and established in Brahman—with fuel in hand.

Apart from the one Guru, [the Truth] is inaccessible through yoga-born [wisdom], through the utterances of Vedānta and logic, through various types of scriptures and collections of treatises, or through meditation and other virtuous practices consisting of mere intellectual reflection.
In the Śivarahasya: "There is nothing superior to the Guru, nothing superior to the Guru, nothing superior to the Guru, nothing superior to the Guru;
this is known, known, known, known from the teaching of Śiva."
In the three worlds filled with Śiva-nature, living beings never attained that state of Śiva;
yet through the sight of the Guru, they attained Śiva-nature. Therefore, the Guru is Śiva, and the Guru alone is the Guru.
Likewise, in the Skanda [Purāṇa]:
"The supreme state, the clearly manifest penetration of Śambhu, which is to be personally realized—that knowledge is to be known from a true Guru; not otherwise, even by millions of scriptures."
Not from logic, nor from the knowledge of words, nor from ritual conduct, nor from the recitation of the Vedas;
not from mantras, nor from [the study of] grammatical characteristics, nor by forceful breath-retention.
Neither by the utterance of the syllable "Haṃsa" nor by the contemplation of the identity of the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman.
Neither from hearing the Vedānta,
nor from the realization of "That thou art," nor from self-restraint, nor from renunciation, nor even from the observance of the stages of life (āśramas) [is liberation attained].
The supreme state is not attained by wearing the six marks of a mendicant, nor by carrying [ascetic] attire, nor by shaving the head,
nor by the exertion of endless means.
For those who are worthy recipients of the guru’s glance— those who are steadfast and speakers of truth—
[liberation occurs] through his speaking, or by his glance, or by his presence, or even by his mere observation.
The supreme state is attained perfectly through that which is inexpressible from the Guru;

for this very reason, Śiva has said: "There is nothing higher than the Guru," and so forth. Due to the fear of excessive prolixity, these matters have not been written here. Like the crest-jewel of all the Vedas (*śruti-śiroratna*), whatever is most excellent in each respective birth is called a "jewel" (*ratna*).

It is said [in the *Viśvakośa*]: "The suffix *matup* occurs when there is a relationship of 'belonging to' or 'being in that. [The author] composed—that is, fashioned—the *Pañcaratna*, which is endowed with the most excellent statements from all the Vedas and Upaniṣads. [He was] the elephant-like venerable Sosali Vīraṇārādhya, who is worthy of worship. [This work is] the *Śrutisārapañcaratna*.
The syntactical connection "he performed" (vyadhatta) is to be sought.
This commentary on the *Śrīpañcaratna*, which accords with all the Vedas,
has been composed by one named Revanārādhya under the title *Śrutyarthadīpikā*.
Having read this commentary, there remains nothing further to be studied;
having known that which is to be known, there is no further instruction to be given by teachers that bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

In the venerable Aitareya Upaniṣad: "One should not teach these Saṃhitās to one who does not live with [the teacher] for a long time, nor to one who has lived [with him] for less than a year, nor to one who is not a speaker [of the truth]. Thus says the Teacher, the Teacher.

In the *Śramadyogasāra*: "Whether out of scholarly pride, for the sake of gain, or through negligence, whoever bestows [the teachings] upon one who is unworthy, the curse of a ḍākinī will inevitably fall upon that great thief."
To that disciple who has served them for twelve years with an undistracted mind— calm and observant of the vow of celibacy— to him this should be imparted.

Thus ends the commentary on the *Śrutisārapañcaratna*, a work composed by the venerable Revanārādhya— the son of the venerable Revanasiddheśvara, who was himself the son of the venerable Sosali Vīraṇārādhya, who was proficient in the *Vedavedaśiras*, the *Śivāgamas*, the *Purāṇas*, and other scriptures.

The commentary known as the *Śrutyarthaprakāśikā*, which elucidates the secret meanings proclaimed from the mouths of the venerable Vṛṣendra and others, and is renowned through abundant scriptures such as the illustrious Vedas, Vedānta, Śiva-āgamas, and Purāṇas, is hereby completed.
May there be auspiciousness; salutations to Śiva!
For those men whose minds are self-subdued, the home itself is a grove of asceticism.
King Janaka, though established in sovereignty, was a yogi superior even to Sanaka and the other great sages.
Prosperity!
